review:
Clair Obscur feels like one of those games that shouldn’t exist, but somehow does because a bunch of passionate weirdos decided “yeah, why not?”

The dev story alone is wild:
A French dude who speedruns Sekiro gets tired of his job at Ubisoft and just… quits to make his dream game. He calls his old university buddy, who ends up becoming the lead tech. He finds a musician on SoundCloud who makes the entire OST. He finds a girl on Reddit who agrees to voice the demo for free and she eventually becomes the lead writer.

Then they hire like thirty fresh grads who are all in over their heads but clearly giving it everything they’ve got. And member number thirty-three? A dog. Literally credited as the Happiness Manager in the end credits.
And the crazy part is: the game actually turned out great. Stylish, unique, full of heart, exactly the kind of thing you get when people make something because they want to, not because some exec told them to.

Clair Obscure is a win for gamers and a big, beautiful middle finger to AAA companies that fill their games with garbage and micro transactions.

One of the best movies I've seen, featuring probably the best soundtrack I've ever heard, yet it manages to unapologetically remind you that it's a video game in the most wild of ways. All wrapped within a resonating lesson on the nature of what it means to be alive. This was a unique experience that I don't anticipate being rivaled for a long time.

Truly a game made by gamers for gamers. Thank you, Sandfall Interactive.

After finishing the game, I used my free time to read a lot of positive and negative reviews.
I saw a lot of negative comments, so I wanted to add my voice to balance that.

I don’t write many reviews. I’m not a hardcore gamer. I’m just a casual player.
I’m not a voice that matters. Just a casual player passing through.
But I still wanted to leave a thank you.

Thank you for sharing your creativity with me. At times it didn’t feel like a game at all... More like walking through an art gallery or an artist’s studio, it was incredible.

If you let this game work on you, it takes you on a creative journey.
The world feels like art. The atmosphere is strong.
It entertained me... And it stayed in my head after playing.

Big respect to the developers. Making games is hard.
And to be honest: modern gamers can be exhausting.
Some negative reviews are so abstract or angry that I don’t even understand their point.
It feels like nothing is ever good enough anymore.

Of course, not every style or genre is for everyone - that’s fair.
But if you like artistic games, mood, and a unique experience, this is worth your time.

Recommended.

[h1][i]"When one falls, we continue."[/i][/h1]

This review is going to sound like it was written by a kid who just finished their very first video game. Which is funny, because it's exactly the opposite. After being a gamer for almost 40 years, I rarely get seriously impressed by a game. If anything, they often feel like a chore, just because of the "been there, done that" effect. But this? This is... Wow. Or should I say "owowow?"

Anyway, our story begins with Ubisoft, the company known for its greed and copy/pasted games. And our hero, Guillaume Broche, grew tired of that. He wanted creativity, not just a paycheck. He left. And he wasn't alone. Another Ubisoft employee, Tom Guillermin, left with him, and since Tom knew Unreal Engine, they started fooling around with it. Things started to take form, and we got an early draft called Sandfall (originally, the game was supposed to revolve around time). But clearly, they needed more people, so... they wrote on Reddit (that was the scale, a bloody Reddit post). They looked for voice actors, but instead, they found their lead writer—Jennifer Svedberg-Yen. And she...

OK, it's hard to describe the story of the game without spoiling it (actually, the one who included certain scenes in the trailer is a criminal). Again, with too many games behind me, I'm rarely excited about stories in video games. Heck, I'm one of those people who hated Last of Us, just because of all the "Will you shut up already? I want to shoot something!" Clair Obscur? Blew me away. Think MYST. Think Cornelia Funke's Inkheart novels, but also think something absolutely unique and beautiful. And also sad. Very sad. Like Cyberpunk 2077 (you can say a lot of things about that game, but it had some really good characters, and its story made a lot of impact because of how things were never fair), Clair Obscur pays so much attention to characters (without making things boring) that it's literally impossible not to care. And when you begin caring? The game will break your freakin' heart. Welcome to Clair Obscur, guys. A world of infinite sadness. Sadness so thick you can feel it with your skin. Which is... Shocking. Not because it's good (it is, though; both the story and atmosphere here are absolutely amazing), but because... Jennifer never wrote for video games. Heck, her previous job didn't even involve writing! Yet here we are. One of the most beautiful stories I've seen in ages.

And you know what? It wasn't just Jennifer. Sandfall (even though the game wasn't about time anymore, Guillaume and Tom kept the name and gave it to the company they co-founded) hired another person with no experience—Lorien Testard. Who's Lorien? Well, he's a guitar teacher who worked on music for fun and posted tracks on SoundCloud. That's it. That's our guy behind the music. Means we've got a cute, yet simple soundtrack, right? Wrong. No, seriously, you couldn't be more wrong. With the help of soprano singer Alice Duport-Percier, Lorien created one of the most beautiful soundtracks I've heard in my entire life. It's not a paid review, but honestly, it's one of those cases when you simply must buy yourself a soundtrack. It's one of a kind, and it's impossible to forget it. You [i]will[/i] keep listening to it long after you finish the game.

Finally, a couple of words about visuals. And it's yet another name that changed the project's look entirely. Originally, in its times as Sandfall, Clair Obscur was a Victorian steampunk. Hence, hiring Nicholas Maxson-Francombe, an illustrator known for such stuff, was logical. I mean, he's another one with no experience with video games whatsoever, but it still made sense. The thing is though, while looking at some random pictures he made, Guillaume understood that those are much more beautiful than what the team had in mind originally. Nicholas for the game's visuals is what Jennifer is for the story. It's hard to describe what he did specifically, but... let's just say he somehow captured a certain kind of [i]magic[/i] in his design. Thanks to him, the game has its own face, its own signature design. Unique and instantly recognizable.

But OK, for a person who believes that gameplay is the most important part, I talked too much about story, music, and visuals. What about the gameplay? Well, what we have here is JRPG. And yes, this game is not Japanese. It's French. Very French. A French aesthetic is everywhere. It's so French that, exactly like I recommend playing Japanese RPGs with the Japanese voices, I recommend playing this one with the French ones. And yes, thanks to the publisher and other financial incomes, English voices here come with the Hollywood cast, but still, I can't imagine this game without the French cast (since you can simply switch to it in options, it looks like it was suggested by the devs too). Yet it's JRPG. Because somehow JRPG became a genre's name, and JRPGs that were not made in Japan have been a thing for quite some time (Septerra Core anyone?).

And you know what? It's yet another cool thing about this game. Let's just admit it, JRPGs are struggling now. Lots of them feel exactly the same (like those games from the Idea Factory, for example), while major franchises like Final Fantasy are going through one heck of an identity crisis. Personally, I used to love those up until PS2 times, where the gameplay changed so much that the games became something entirely different. Clair Obscur? In a way, it's what Final Fantasy wants to be but fails. It's also important to remember another Square-Enix title – The Legend of Dragoon. Remember how that game used a smart workaround to make turn-based battles more dynamic? Clair Obscur does the same. And it goes all the way into that direction. Despite being turn-based, it wants you to dodge, parry, and even jump during the battles. Which makes it feel almost real-time at times. And it feels... Awesome.

No, seriously. The battles here feel almost like something from the rhythm games. Remember good ol' Patapon? That's the stuff. When it's about those big bosses, you either pon-pon-patapon their attacks or die. And it's not just a coincidence, it's by design. On many occasions, the characters will compare battles to dances. Like everything else in this game, battles are bloody art. And so is the leveling mechanics.

Personally, I don't like overly complicated mechanics. Sitting on my butt and doing micromanagement for hours instead of exploring and fighting? Not really my thing. Clair Obscur? It can pleasure both people like me [i]and[/i] the micromanagement crowd. Long story short, things revolve around some items called "pictos." Those are the things you can equip on your characters for certain effects (like Materia in Final Fantasy). What's interesting here is that those chain. Here's an example: There's that ultimate boss who can and will one-hit-kill you. What can you do about it? Well, you can equip certain pictos. One will instantly resurrect you and give you a second chance, another gives you some buff upon being resurrected, and the third one will give the boss a debuff. Do pictos right and you'll be able to one-hit-kill every single enemy in this game, including that ultimate boss. Which is extremely satisfying.

And again, it was intentional. Clair Obscur's developers weren't just making a game. They were making a game they wanted to play for themselves. You can feel it everywhere. In how very special and personal the story is, in how beautiful the music is... Even the gameplay is full of some little touches it's hard not to praise. For example, my biggest problem with the genre is that battle animations are very long and the UI is too bulky. Sandfall guys? They felt the same. Thanks to which battles, despite being extremely spectacular, are also pretty fast-paced. So yeah. What we have here is not just GOTY, it's the best game I've played in, like, a decade. You either love Clair Obscur or you just didn't play it yet. It's simple like that.

Just play it blind. Don't look up anything in regards to the game until credits roll. I promise you won't regret it.

The most beautiful game I have ever played, in every aspect! I think by now everyone has played or at least heard about Clair Obscure: Expedition 33, but I'm not going to spoil anything about the game in this review. The story is about a group of people living in an isolated town called Lumiere, inspired by France during the Belle Époque. A huge number can be seen on the monolith that the Paintress paints every year, which affects them, so they form a team of expeditioners to sail to her in hopes of killing her and stopping her from harming the people in Lumiere. This year, Expedition 33 is gathering to start the adventure. Will they be able to stop her and live life normally?
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3735188216

The gameplay is like that of old RPGs, where you explore a world map, travel from city to city, meet people, kill monsters, and upgrade your weapons. The fighting is turn-based, which I'm familiar with. Think of old Final Fantasy games when you play this game. It is clear it was inspired by those old games, and the atmosphere is similar to NieR, which is one of my favorite games. However, there is no manual save; the game autosaves regularly. Whenever you find a flag checkpoint, it will save automatically and let you fast-travel to another checkpoint. Make sure to touch the checkpoint flag whenever you want to save. 

The combat is turn-based with QTEs, which you can set to auto in the settings if that's not your thing. Each character has a different fighting style and set of skills. The only things I had to do repeatedly were parrying attacks and dodging. I found out that by learning and hearing the attack, it would be easy to parry it. It frustrated me a couple of times, especially with some bosses you can't kill unless you parry them, but you can always fail and learn how to do it next time. The game needs some grinding to kill some bosses. Try not to skip any monsters you see around; kill them to level up and earn new weapons.  
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3735506708

The artwork is outstanding, and every detail in the game is beautiful and meaningful. The color palette chosen for each area is mesmerizing, and the character's design is memorable. This game did something other games in my opinion failed to do. There is no UI and clutter while you are exploring the areas; you just walk around and enjoy each detail without having a health bar, a minimap, or a distracting list of objectives. You have the full screen to yourself and your character, which is a huge plus for me, as it lets me enjoy the environment.

The characters' animations and facial expressions are on point; you can see the emotions in their gazes, posture, and voices. The voice actors did an outstanding job capturing the essence of those characters. It felt like watching a movie; in each scene, you could see how they reacted, what they looked like, and how they received each piece of information. This alone makes you want to replay the game to watch those little details. The dialogues are extremely well written.   
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3735805052

Music is breathtakingly beautiful; each soundtrack is meaningful; the lyrics tell a story and capture the characters' emotions. The game has 154 tracks on the main album alone, worth listening to, and they will actually stick in your head after playing the game.    

Character development is one of the strong suits of this game; you can see and feel how they bond, how they become stronger, how they hate, and how they grow suspicious. The writing of each character is phenomenal, especially in Act 2.   

Pros:
+Emotional beautiful story.
+Outstanding soundtracks.
+Beautiful graphics and animations.
+Great characters and monsters design.
+Phenomenal voice over.
+Turn-based combat.
+World map.
+Fast traveling.
+Journal.
+Multiple endings.
+Collectables.
+Cosmatics for each character.
+Auto save.
+Steam achievements.

Cons:
- No manual save.


The game is unique in that it doesn't explain the story to you directly; it wants you to follow it emotionally and logically, forming theories about what is going on before the grand reveal. I highly recommend not charging and just killing bosses without exploring the world, reading the journals, or speaking to the characters. Those interactions will give you different layers to the story, and you'll understand it more, especially in the last act, where you'll be able to explore the whole map to read more information and learn more about the characters. The game has two endings; it is up to you how you want this to end.

I’m playing games for 3 decades now, and Clair Obscur is one of the best I experienced in all of this time. Of course I got all the excitement about it, and all the positive reviews and how much people loved it, but I honestly still did not expect it to be this good…
   
[u][b]Story[/b][/u]   
The game takes place in a surreal, painterly fantasy world, where art, architecture, and technology mix together in an elegant and dreamlike way. But as beautiful as the world is, it comes at a steep price. Society is built around a single horrifying phenomenon: a mysterious being called the Paintress.
Each year, the Paintress paints a number onto a distant monolith. When that happens, every person of that exact age instantly disappears turning into a cloud of flower pedals.
Because of this, humanity lives with a constant sense of countdown and inevitability of when their deaths will happen. Families know the year their loved ones will disappear, and the world has reorganized itself around this grim cycle.
To try to end the curse, the remaining cities send out Expeditions - groups of volunteers who journey across the dangerous lands toward the Paintress. But so far…none have succeeded. 
  
Expedition 33…
The story follows Expedition 33, the newest team sent to attempt the impossible: find the Paintress and stop the cycle before their own time runs out.
Members of the expedition know they may not return, but they still set out across a strange continent filled with ruined civilizations, bizarre creatures, and environments that feel like living paintings.
On their travels they uncover fragments of past expeditions and clues about the deeper nature of the world and learn more about the fate of the expeditions that came before them. 
  
[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]   
It is a mix of talking to your fellow expeditioners, and learning more about each other, exploring big, semi open world levels. (I say semi open world, since there are different routes, but most level contain several routes you can follow that loop back on each other, which is by no means a bad thing!!!, quite the opposite) 
The different areas are connected via an overworld map, which you unlock more and more of, while you progress the story.   
When it comes to battle, Clair Obscur turns into a turned based battle mode which happens in the world, but can involve different number of enemies, from my experience it isn’t always just the ones you see. 
For each character you have different options, either attack normally to increase your AP (which is needed for stronger skills), use items or execute one of your many skills. 
Nearly every skill in this game different effects added to it, like for a simple example, cause a burn status effect on the enemy, while other party members have attacks that do more damage on enemies with this status effect. But of course, there are countless different combinations and possibilities to take into consideration when making your moves, which makes the battle system very intuitive but also adds a lot of complexity with time. 
Furthermore, another big part of the fights are the active dodging mechanic and quick time events for your skills. Many skills allow for increased damage, or extend buffs when you hit these. 
Once an enemy starts attack you, you have the option to either dodge the attack or parry it, which happens in real time, it can take a while to learn the right pattern for each attack, but once you figured it out and managed to actively counter or avoid the enemy attacks, it feels extremely satisfying! 
   
[u][b]Graphic/Audio/Atmosphere[/b][/u]
Clair Obscur has probably the best and most creative level design I personally ever experienced. The amount of love, creativity and details flown into the look, feeling and environment, and animations to make the world be more alive is second to none. They went all out with the concept that this world I painted. Absolutely every area of this game is an absolute masterpiece, I can’t describe it in any other way. 

And oh my gosh…the soundtrack, to say it is stunning and beautiful is an understatement, each song is sung with so much passion and fits so perfectly all the time, sometimes you just stop, close your eyes and listen. 

Same can be said for the general sound design of the game, attacks, environment, character movement, etc…it just all fits perfectly and sounds amazing, they hasn’t been a single sound that I started to dislike, even when hearing it countless times…it is hard to call something like this perfect…but for this game, I would go that far. 
  
[u][b]Tech[/b][/u]  
The game is, from what I experienced of course, very well optimized, and mostly ran fluently, I had like 1 or 2 crashes in over 100 hours of gameplay, and I think even these are mostly because of my system. So no complains there. 
 
[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]  
Even if turned base combat isn’t your thing, I would argue Clair Obscur: Expedtion 33 is one of these very rare must-play games. The world, story, characters, creative ideas, world design and combat system mix so well together. Clair Obscur is one of the rare cases where a game will stay with you for a while, even after you watched the credits. 
One of the best gaming experiences I had in my entire life.

Lost Odyssey, Nier, and Shadow Hearts tossed in a blender with Sekiro's parry. This game is incredible, and possibly the single greatest thing to come out of France since the invention of the croissant

It brought back a sense of wonder and an excitement for things to come that I haven't felt since I was a kid playing RPGs on the Super Nintendo. I don't know what arcane French magic they concocted to achieve this, but I loved every moment of it. Not just my favorite game this year, one of my favorite games ever.

Alright. [i]Clair Obscur: Expedition 33[/i] is done and dusted. For me, this game mostly lived up to the hype, which is always nice to see. It had some incredibly intense holy -ish moments, some tear-soaked moments, and just some all-around crazy moments. Often all three crashed together, lol. The game itself is an interesting mix of open world and linear JRPG with a WRPG flair, FromSoft style Soulsborne concepts and UI, and The Last of Us 1/2 Influenced writing. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3653462158

The prologue itself gives you an inkling of the emotional roller coaster ride you are about to embark on. You play as Gustave who is about to watch as the woman he loves but had broken up with, is about to be Gomagged (erased). Which is this world's version of people dying when they're a certain age, on the day the Paintress reduces the number on the horizon by one. So, this year, everyone who is 34 dies when she changes the number to 33. Next year, it would be 32, and so on. So, you are given an emotionally heavy moment from the very beginning of the game, lol. To me, this prologue was equally intense compared to TLOU 1's prologue, and I can't think of another game that even comes close.

The day after the Gommage each year, the people of Lumiere send an expedition to try and stop the Paintress. This is the 67th year they've done so. This expedition, Expedition 33, features Lumiere's bravest from the group of 33-year-olds who will of course be Gommaged next year anyway. So, Gustave and his friends, along with his 16-year-old ward, Maelle, set off on said expedition. When they finally land on the mainland, things get completely insane. You are treated to the first of many holy -ish moments right there. And then the prologue ends and you are properly in the game.

With the impression the prologue leaves, you already know this game is going to be insane, and by and large, that holds true. I thought the writing was stellar most of the way through the game. And you know what I said about the Prologue being insane. That can't even match what happens at the end of Act One, lol. I was actually stunned by that transition and had to stop and reflect on it for a bit. Again, the Druckmann influence shows up in spades here. I actually was in disbelief of what had just happened, and I was impressed that Sandfall was gutsy enough to take the story there.

Where I think there is a drop off in the writing is in the game's conclusion. It's not bad by any stretch of the imagination. Actually, it's quite good. But...I think it lost a bit of the seamless progression that the writing enjoyed prior to that, and kind of bogged down a bit. I kept thinking during Act Three that the pacing shifted a bit too much and dragged on more than I would have personally liked. It was important to have this conclusion and the two end story options, but the pacing definitely suffered for the final reveals and overall exposition. Memorable, but not on par with the rest of the game. In my opinion.

Gameplay is a mix of overland open world travel; and linear exploration with a few branching paths to find secrets and items, when in specific areas. As you expand your list of companions, and their power grows, your ability to unlock more of the open world map really starts to show off the size of this world, which is reasonably large, with plenty of required AND plenty of optional areas to explore. I have 29 hours put into this game, but if you are thorough, you can easily get 70+ hours out of the game just based on exploration alone. 

The named areas in the game are mostly linear, as mentioned above. There is always a main path to follow with maybe a couple side path shortcuts included, and a degree of interconnectivity within each map that touches on the FromSoft formula of world building a bit. There will typically also be side paths that lead to secrets, be they items, past expedition logs, and even optional bosses. And some of those side paths actually lead to what are essentially full dungeons. So, it's not a bad idea to try and explore as much as you like.

Scattered along the way in each area, you will find past Expedition flags. Those serve as traditional Soulsborne bonfires, where you will level up, learn new skills, rest and heal; and late game, they are also used to upgrade gear AND your party member's Lumina/Pictos, which is basically a set of innate combat skills/buffs that can be unlocked by spending Lumina points. Prior to gear upgrades and Lumina unlocking at the flags, there will be an NPC that shows up at your camps after a certain point in the story who will handle those two things for you. That NPC can also upgrade your flasks (basically the same system you find in Elden Ring, but with the addition of a resurrection flask as well).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3647194469

You can only camp on the overland map, but it is important as, in addition to upgrading your Lumina and weapons (and flasks), this is also where you will build relationships with your companions, get some more lore about the world, and a couple other camp options that will be unlocked as well. You also have a record player in camp and can enjoy any music you may have found in your travels already. 

Which, the soundtrack for this game is flat out stunning. Unquestionably one of the best OSTs to ever grace a video game. And since we're talking audio, everything was as good as it gets here. From the voice acting to the in-game sounds, the sounds in combat....all of it was top top tier. Sandfall put the industry on notice with the excellence of the audio in this game.

And the exact same is true of the visuals. I defy you to play this game and not take several hundred screenshots. This game is literally THAT gorgeous. This was an amazing job the artists for Sandfall did here. Again, they pretty much put the gaming industry on notice with this one.

Sandfall talks about the reactive turn-based combat system on the product page. This was a pretty innovative system IMO. It is standard JRPG shootout style, BUT...it features attack and defense QTE's and an action point system. The QTEs mirror the type of combat options you directly get in Soulsborne games. Dodging, parrying, jumping, timing your attacks properly, and so on. It's a little jarring seeing those systems implemented in a turn-based game, but it definitely works. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3653462349

That said, I didn't love the attack part of this. Which Sandfall clearly understood would be a sticking point for a lot of gamers. So, there is an option to disable the attack QTEs. Which I did. You can't disable the defense QTEs, however, and actually as I played, I really started to understand why. The dodging and parrying (and jumping) is integral to other mechanics baked into combat. So, you will just have to learn enemy movements and windups and do your best to get your timing down. Which wasn't really so difficult IMO. You won't always be right, but it's incredibly satisfying when you get that chain of parries, and doing so gives you enough action points to pull off one of your epic nine-point abilities. This was a pretty robust and fun system. 

Obviously, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is a must play. And it's definitely priced fairly for the amount of content there is in the game, not to mention the absolutely industry breaking sound and art design. Is it flawless? No. And in reality, I was exhausted by the end. But I'll also remember this game and think back upon it often.

[spoiler]On the surface it looks like a gorgeous game about stopping an apocalypse. But underneath that it's a story about a mother who couldn't let go of her dead son, a father destroying an entire world to save his wife from herself, and a daughter caught between two lives wondering which one is actually hers. Nobody here is a villain. Everyone is just broken in their own way and trying to survive it.

Then there's Verso. A painted copy of a dead boy, fully aware that he is not real. He never asked to exist. He just woke up one day inside someone else's pain and had to figure out what to do with that. He spends decades watching people die, loses the person he loved, grows tired of everything, and eventually decides the kindest thing he can do is end it all. Not out of hatred. Out of pure exhaustion. And his own mother, when she finally sees him, looks him in the eyes and says: [i]you are not my Verso.[/i] After a century of feeling and losing and carrying all of it. Still just a copy.

And somewhere in the canvas a faceless little boy wanders alone, painting endlessly, keeping the whole world alive. Everyone made decisions around him, about him, for him. The only one who ever bothered to ask what he wanted was Verso himself.

The game never lets you feel comfortable. It builds people you care about and then asks you to decide their fate. Do you save a painted world full of people who laugh, love and die just like anyone else? Or do you free a soul that has been trapped inside it since the day he died?[/spoiler]

Neither answer is clean. The game doesn't pretend otherwise.

[i]Life keeps forcing cruel choices.[/i] No other game has made me feel the weight of that sentence the way this one did.

Without a doubt a game of the year contender and honestly a winner. What Sandfall Interactive created here is an absolute masterpiece.

I never played turn based action games before and this was a perfect introduction. I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to get into turn based action or turn based JRPG style games. It feels welcoming but still deep and rewarding.

The visuals are stunning. Face capture animations feel incredibly real and expressive. After watching some behind the scenes videos it is honestly insane how much work went into body language and facial mimics. Areas like Lumiere and the Forgotten Battlefield look breathtaking and make the world feel heavy, alive and meaningful. The art direction deserves special praise because every location feels hand crafted with a clear emotional tone rather than just being pretty. Performance was smooth for me and the UI is clean and readable without breaking immersion.

The music is a masterpiece on its own. I constantly paused the game just to listen to the beautiful menu soundtrack. My favorite tracks are Gustave theme, The Departure and the absolutely goated Monoco theme. The soundtrack elevates every emotional moment and stays with you long after you stop playing.

Gameplay wise the game does a great job. Some mechanics do get repetitive and certain broken builds can make the game feel repetitive in terms of moves and animations. Seeing the same animations over and over can get a bit stale. That said the dodge and parry mechanics combined with the aim system add enough engagement to keep combat exciting. Enemy variety is fantastic with so many unique movesets to learn and overcome. Simon stands as the pinnacle of everything the game teaches you throughout its length and is an unforgettable challenge.

Story wise this is straight up peak fiction and it leaves you wanting more. I got deeply invested in the world of Expedition 33 and tears were definitely not rare while playing. The game celebrates victories and mourns losses in a very human way. If I learned anything from this journey it is the importance of caring for those who come after us. I will not spoil the story or its twists but witnessing it all made me rethink what makes a person real, what it means to be alive and what consciousness truly is. The more I write the more memories come back and the more I want to say, but out of respect for the story I will stop here.

My absolute favorite characters are Sciel and Gustave. Sciel really clicked with me and offered a powerful perspective on death and the afterlife that will probably stay with me for a lifetime. If there is an afterlife then I will see everyone after death. And if there is not I will simply join them in death. I will be with them either way. Gustave on the other hand teaches the importance of caring for others and working on yourself so you can help people in the long run. Campsite interactions are a brilliant feature that truly helps you connect with the characters and understand their motivations. I am genuinely grateful that I got to experience these characters and their stories.

All in all this game is an emotional rollercoaster that deserves to be played. It is without a doubt a game of the year winner for me(2025). I heavily recommend it even if you are not a turn based enjoyer. Buy it at full price and you will not regret a cent, at least I did not. What started as curiosity quickly turned into one of the most memorable experiences I’ve had in a long time.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
Absolutely stunning.

The lighting, environmental design, effects, textures, and animations all come together beautifully. The level design, in particular, sometimes pleasantly reminded me of Alice: Madness Returns, with creative layouts and visually striking areas.

Every location feels carefully crafted and visually unique, and I spent a ton of time in photo mode capturing the world from different angles.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Audio[/h2]
One of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard in a video game.

[b]My personal top tracks:[/b]
[olist]
    [*]Aria pour un Masque de Colère
    [*]Lumière
    [*]The Reacher – Orphelin
[/olist]

Sound design is also top-notch; everything feels crisp and impactful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Very good. Each character has a unique combat style, which really reinforces their personality.

The gameplay feels like it has two layers. On one hand, you can build a powerful setup and dominate enemies. On the other hand, even without optimal builds, you can rely on skill, dodging or parrying with good timing to win fights.

I really loved how they implemented it. Despite the large number of battles, combat never got boring throughout the entire game.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Hard to talk about without spoilers.

All I’ll say is that it’s unique, engaging, and memorable. The main characters are charismatic, each with their own personality, motivations, and backstories, and they act in believable ways.

The ending leaves a strong impression.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cons[/h2]
[h3]Lumina progression system[/h3]
I didn’t really like how Luminas are leveled. You need to use a newly obtained Lumina in several battles before it becomes permanently available. This makes build-crafting awkward because you constantly have to swap them in just to level them up. It would feel much better if they could be upgraded using Chroma instead.

[h3]Too many Luminas / balance issues[/h3]
By the end of the game, there are just too many Luminas. They become hard to manage and, more importantly, they break the balance. Characters become extremely overpowered, to the point where story bosses, which are supposed to be important and strong, feel easier than early-game enemies when you had almost nothing.

Meanwhile, the “hardcore” bosses in the Endless Tower feel less like a fair challenge and more like a clunky way to counter overpowered builds.

[h3]World map navigation[/h3]
Not very convenient, and could be better. A minimap or markers would help a lot.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
These minor flaws didn’t stop me from enjoying the game at all.

Most of the time, I didn’t even think about them — I was too engaged in the story, combat, exploration, and the beautiful world.

Sandfall Interactive has created one of the most artful and inspired games in years with E33, which is peak irony considering this studio is made up of former Ubisoft devs. It shows just how much corporate money men and playing it safe can stifle creative expression and freedom, as when set free to create this is the kind of masterpiece Ubisoft developers can create when unleashed. 

I do think this is one of the few games of each generation that is a must play, from the music to the artistic styling, this game is a beautiful experience that feels fresh in a sea of generic and safe AAA and even AA products. 

This is high praise from me, someone who doesn’t really enjoy turn based combat (outside of deck builders). At least you have dodging, parries and QTE interactions (that I admit I lazily chose the auto option for), along with an absolutely massive selection of potential builds to keep the combat feeling interactive and varied. By the end I had so many ‘Pictos’ (abilities) mastered the build potential was overwhelming – perfectly set up for a future play-through. Though after a 100% play-through, I likely never will do NG+, for reasons mentioned later. 

Overall I quite enjoyed the story, it has everything from highly emotionally charged moments, to humour to anger inducing desires to see revenge carried out. Though I do think it falls off a bit in the later parts and after the main story it is mostly nonsense, to be honest. 

I really have to give credit to both the music and artistic styling in this game, it really is stunning and I enjoyed every aspect of these. It again highlights how talented devs are so often creatively stifled when in big companies like Ubisoft, but can produce incredible content when they are allowed the creative freedom to do so. 

On the downside, many of the enemies feel repeated and some are pretty much all the way through the game. If you dislike the combat, you’re going to be really drained by the end of the game. I chose to get 100% on this game (special thanks to Optinoob on YT for his guides!) and honestly by the end I was so over it I was literally avoiding combat unless absolutely necessary. That being said, if you absolutely loved the main campaign, then you’re getting an absolute bargain with the huge number of optional areas and bosses to fight. 

I have to be clear, my fatigue was result of going for 100% achievements and most people will never feel this way just playing the main story part of the game. 

I would recommend the main campaign to anyone and everyone, if you love gaming and appreciate artistic styling with very quirky music accompanying the journey, you will love this and again I do think this is one of those rare ‘must play’ games.

I bought this game to cope with the fact that I will lose a parent within the next couple of months. I needed a way to escape from reality momentarily, so nothing better than choosing a game with death, loss and grief as it's central themes, right? In the end, I have become addicted to it.

The story has been touching right from the start and I can easily say that it has one of the most outstanding intros to a game that I have got to experience in recent years. You get to care and almost cry for characters that you have only known for 30 minutes. The use of narrative elements is quite beautiful too and it often feels like watching a movie. Over the course of the story, you will get to know how other people in this world deal with grief; some manage to move on, others will be stuck in it forever. You won't be able to understand it until you have gone through it yourself and that aspect heavily influences your perception of the story.

The combat is extremely fun, yet challenging. Mastering timings and enemy patterns feels extremely rewarding and there's also a decent amount of end-game content to spend time with. The visuals are absolutely stunning and the music made me start playing my piano again after neglecting it for a while due to burnout. Without a doubt one of the best gaming OSTs out there. If there's one thing I disliked, it is the option to have some romantic dialogue with two of your companions. That felt very out of place considering the setting and several other factors. It is completely optional though and doesn't affect the story.

Genuinely one of the few games I have played that made me realize how beautiful life can be sometimes, even in times of hardship, if it means that I get to experience this work of art. It shows how much a small team can accomplish, as long as they show love and appreciation for their craft.

A masterpiece of art disguised as a game, I cannot recommend it enough. 
If I ever start forgetting things, I hope to stumble upon this review, just to experience the story once more.

I literally had no idea about this game last year when it released. I just thought it would be a random turn-based game from unknown developers. There was little to no hype for this game, as it wasn’t one of those AAA IPs we are already familiar with. But then came The Game Awards 2025—this game got nominated for Game of the Year. I was shocked, as it was competing with some of the greatest games released that year, like KCD 2, Hades 2, as well as Silksong. But when the day came, it literally swept almost every award, and the next month it overtook Elden Ring to become the most awarded game of all time. My mind was completely blown away by the success of this unfamiliar title, so I decided to give it a try through Game Pass.

First of all, if you are planning to buy this game, play it for free on Game Pass first to get a basic idea of what it’s all about, because it’s not for everyone. Many people may find its real-time turn-based combat boring and repetitive (which is not true in my case). I played Pokémon games for years, and this was a huge upgrade for me, as now we are parrying and dodging enemy attacks rather than just taking them. I never found this game’s combat boring; it always felt fresh to me. Getting new pictos, trying new skills, and making different builds for characters were engaging. This game has so much content—even after finishing the main story, there are many locations, side bosses, and mysteries left to explore. That’s why I purchased this game on Steam even after finishing the main story on Game Pass.

And then comes its music—"OH MY GOD." Every soundtrack in this game is GOATed. Literally, when I opened this game for the very first time, I just sat watching the main screen, listening to its music. From there, I knew it was going to be one of the best games I have ever played, because I absolutely love listening to video game soundtracks. I didn’t understand a single word from it, but the feelings it gave to my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ears were incredible. It’s also shocking that such great soundtracks were composed by an unknown artist hired from SoundCloud. Sometimes I just hum the music of this game when doing nothing.

For the story and characters (NO SPOILERS), it’s the same as the music—"PEAK." I don’t remember the last time I had tears in my eyes while playing a game, and that too within the first hour. There are some games that start off slow and rough but make sense in the end; this game, on the other hand, literally hooked me from start to finish. No fillers—just absolute cinema moments every time. You are not playing this game but living in it. And OMG, the cast—Ben Starr, Jennifer English, Charlie Cox, and Andy Serkis—such a packed lineup. You already knew this was going to be peak. The emotions I felt for them—their fear, joy, and sadness—touched my heart, and I will never forget the beautiful experience this game gave me through its story and characters. This is the pinnacle of storytelling in this form of media. If you play this game in the future, just don’t rush through the story. Always engage in character conversations and optional cutscenes. Even if you completely move on from this game, its story and characters will stay with you forever in your heart.

Now, the gameplay, as mentioned earlier, will not satisfy everyone. But if you have played turn-based games in the past, this game is definitely for you. The Lumina system is excellent—you can stack different abilities and effects to create an OP build. After all the positives I mentioned earlier, the only weakness I feel this game has is that by using the Picto and Lumina systems, the difficulty can feel weak. You become so strong that you can easily beat the main story without even dying. However, the post-main-story content gets a bit harder, and that difficulty spike compensates for the earlier limitation. All I can say is: don’t look for guides—they can ruin your experience.

As this game is made in Unreal Engine 5, it looks visually beautiful, but it can be demanding in terms of hardware. Still, it is optimized—no bugs, glitches, or performance issues. Everything is fine. I can’t believe this was their first game, and they delivered one of the masterpieces of this generation. Now I hope the developers can maintain this level of quality with their future releases.

Final Verdict—
This game is easily in my top three of all time, second only to Elden Ring. The experience it gave me will forever remain in my heart. I wish I could erase my memories of this game so that I could feel those emotions again for the first time. After playing this game, I now understand why it won nine awards at TGA—it completely outshined its competition. Even if you don’t like the gameplay, play it for the story. It is what everybody says—"Absolute Cinema." It’s one of those games you should play before dying. As a wise man once said:

This game is an incredible JRPG experience with so much heart and soul, so much polish, it puts the entire triple A gaming industry to shame. 

Clair Obsecur sculpts its lore around the most core of human emotions. It is a story about the meaning of stories, it is art about the power of art. it is an experience that demands we collectively return to it again and again, not for entertainment, but because it is a story about grief. And our need for art about grief will never disappear. 

And with grief at it's center, the narrative introduces so many concepts whilst still managing to keep them so meaningful. It grounds them in people and in metaphor, bringing them to life on your screen. Its remarkable writing adds a sense of beautiful sensitivity, delicateness and humanity to the characters and their personality. It creates a world so big in its scale of breadth and imagination, yet so small in its emotions and experience. And it does it all without ever losing balance.  

The combat is so satisfying, it revolutionizes the turn-based system, polishing its fundamentals and adds upon it in ways that modernizes the experience. The open world is so thoughtfully constructed, it's directed enough that you always know where you should go and yet open enough that exploration still results in a delightfully earned sense of power fantasy. The Environmental story telling is similarly phenomenal. Every detail gives you a clue into the world and it's history/stories. It rewards you for paying attention and makes your surroundings come alive as you traverse through them.

This game should not exist. It is a project that accomplishes so much with so little. It is an outlier. A droplet of innovation in a sea of soulless corporate mediocrity. Its existence is a contradiction to the industry giants that have long replaced art in video games with corperate greed. This game, by all definitions of the word, is art.

But even art can never be perfect. The combat balance tends to be weak at times. The item descriptions tend to be vague and unclear. There's a lack of quality of life features to help streamline navigation and exploration. The level design feels more like a maze then organic terrain. It's these small details that add up to make a big difference in the overall experience of this game. It is what stops Clair obscur from living up to it's immeasurable praise. And while it's far from a true flawless masterpiece, it's short coming does not come anywhere near enough to take away from its accomplishments.

This game is a rare achievement. It’s ambitious, heartfelt, and unforgettable. And despite its rough edges, its creativity, storytelling, and soul more than makes up for it.

That's why I highly recommend this game.

I shudder at the knowledge that it took me this long to get around and play this game. I had it on my radar, of course, but at the sudden announcement of FF7 Rebirth, I caved. And this game has spent the last 60+ hours making me regret that decision. Multiple times.

[h1]A blank canvas[/h1]

Sandfall Interactive is a relatively small studio, and while some work has been offloaded to external companies, it's impressive that such a small team was able to accomplish so much.
The story behind the team is nothing short of inspiring. 
From a single person leaving Ubisoft chasing a passion project and opening a new studio, to the process of hiring the talent from social media and Reddit posts, and lastly obtaining funding, it's genuinely a level of dedication you don't see often.
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (E33) is their first title, and, my God: what an opener.

I won't get too much into the story, as I believe anything I say might ruin the - and I'm mincing my words - masterfully crafted narrative, but I can say the writing has been up there with some of the best work I've had the pleasure to experience. I have always been on the edge of my seat, while having a laugh, as the game doesn't always take itself so seriously, abeit it is, being unequivocally French in themes and humor. 
A story this captivating isn't something that often happens, and while E33 does not reinvent the wheel, the wheel is perfect as it is, and it's presented incredibly.

The cast of characters, especially, are a standout. Well written, and with their own point of view, coherent for the entire runtime. I've loved the night camp mechanic straight out of Dragon Age Origins and the relationship tiers of Persona, which made me fall in love with them even more. A stellar cast, and an even more stellar performance from all of them. 

From afar, the game seems to be a turn-based game heavily influenced by the Persona series, especially in its UI, but when looking harder, the influence of other titles can be seen. For example, the timed attacks and dodging were a defining aspect of Mario and Luigi RPGs, and the addition of a parry Sekiroes up the experience, differentiating it from any other game in the genre I ever played, where I often end up somewhat distracted during the turns of the enemies, especially later in the game.

The combat is genuinely addicting, and with the way the game is structured, I never found fighting a drag, but always something I engaged with as much as possible; although I must say the lack of a way to avoid low-level fights like in Metaphor Re-Fantazio, or the Persona series when unlocking the ability, was definitely felt.

I especially enjoyed how different each character's skill set is, covering many roles for each of them, and yet allowing huge build variety. The amount of Pictos - abilities that can either be slotted when unknown, or equipped at a cost freely once mastered - is honestly overwhelming. Especially when considering that everything stacks cumulatively in the game, an aspect I don't believe many players, unless they interact with the endgame, ever come across. 

This goes to show even more how tailored to many different people the game is, from story-focused to hardcore endgame, there is something for everybody. Especially since additional content was released with the Thank You update.

The art style of the game seems to have taken a page out of From Software's handbook, with each area looking straight out of a painting, and with a very strong design identity, making the more realistic presentation everything but bland.
There are many ideas that stand out as fitting and clever; for example, the traversal of the world map happening in a pseudo-diorama of the world has to be my favorite. It really helps to feel the dimension of the continent, while providing character to something that usually has been just functional. 

Last but not least, the soundtrack is a magical 8h of composition. I am, weeks later from my completion of the game, still listening to.
It establishes itself with some motifs that are then used during the entire game to communicate to the player, subconsciously, things that they are not aware of yet. A little bit like the Advent Children's musical cues and motifs when Sephiroth appears in the new FF7 Remakes; it hints at something that, if you know: you know.
Additionally, carefully hiding the meaning of the game in many lyrics, behind not just the French language, but a cypher built from pseudo‑Latin phrasing, invented vocabulary, and layered symbolism designed to obscure the narrative, is the cherry on top. 

[h1]Unreal, despite Unreal[/h1]

The game has been developed using Unreal Engine 5, and while I appreciate that its existence is allowing small teams such as this to develop a title of this caliber that in the past we might have seen only from AAA studios like Naughty Dog, I must say it has to be its biggest flaw, while not being of the game in the first place.

The thing is this.
There aren't many options on the market, besides UE5 and Unity; the latter could never have delivered at this level.
Indeed, there are other engines that can compete well with UE5. 
For example, Anvil by Ubisoft has implemented virtualized geometry, or Decima used by Kojima and Guerrilla, and the RE Engine - when Capcom optimizes their games. But all of them have one thing in common: they are non-licenseable. 
Could Sandfall have spent years making an engine? Sure, but that wasn't profitable for Konami with MGS:V, let alone a brand new studio.
Therefore, UE5 is the pick, and while Sandfall tried their best to avoid many of the common issues like just-in-time shader compilation or traversal stutters, with it come many of the issues of the engine. Please bear in mind, I do [b]not[/b] fault Sandfall for them, as these are present in all games made in the engine. 

Character motion, while well done, results in floaty and imprecise. Especially when turning, the characters lose no momentum whatsoever. Far from me to say that every engine should break the ankles of its characters like From Software does to establish contact with the ground, but even in the intro of E33 it's possible to see Gustave's feet are clipping in the slightly angled roofs; something that [url=https://gamingpastime.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/assassinscreed2_4.jpg]wasn't an issue in 2009[/url]. 

Clutter around the map has very precise collisions, which, combined with the motion, often end up dead-stopping your momentum, for example, on a candle holder. Additionally, a lot of items have been made using virtualized geometry - nanite. For example, the stairs in some buildings or small decor, that, because of nanite collapse logic, end up looking more poligon-y than a PS2 game. There are not a lot of physics-enabled items, besides boxes, making the world of the game stunning to look at, yet not so interactive. 

Lighting is handled via Software Lumen, and somehow, in 2025, the abovementioned minor items are not being properly ambient occluded or shaded, leading to a lot of clutter that looks floating because they are not included in the simplified SDFs used for the lighting. 

All things considered, the cost of rendering versus the - stunning - end result, especially for a static world, is just bonkers. Especially when a simple option in the engine to rasterize all this real-time info would have solved it. 

And while I don't agree with many of his takes or tone, this [url=https://youtu.be/Ls4QS3F8rJU]video[/url] goes in depth about the rendering issues the game has, despite Sandfall's efforts.

[h1]Varnished[/h1]

As a final note on the review, despite the engine limitations usually being a turn-off for me, the game exceeded my expectations and has become a magical experience that, honestly, I will think fondly of for a long time.

I'm glad they were able to bring this to life, and I can't wait to see what they work on next.

Overall this is a great game, and if you can get it on sale it's definitely worth the money. 

At it's core this game is just like any other traditional RPG game with menu fighting. It's similar in that regard to games like Final Fantasy, or older games like Chrono Trigger. 

In the menu RPG category what this game does differently is add a lot of quick time events (QTE) and timed parry requirements to fights. A lot of people enjoy those menu fighting RPG games because of how relaxed they can be since they give you the ability to calmly fight and pay less attention to the screen. The QTE and parry requirements do make it so you are encouraged to stay focused and react quickly which can turn some people off. There is an easy mode where if you crank up your defense you can ignore a lot of things, but even on easy there are encounters and bosses you won't be able to do unless you can nail those timed parry events. 

The world and soundtrack are amazing. Many will find the story to be great, but others will find the story slowly gets worse over time and lackluster at the end. I found the story gave a lot of plot slowly in the beginning, then it was like all characters for the longest time refused to talk about anything story related with substance until it was nearly the end of the game. It dragged out the mystery so long that I personally lost interest, which made the ending a little more underwhelming. 

For me the best part of the game was the beginning, and then being allowed to explore such a beautiful world. I had fun taking my time exploring every area, killing every monster, and enjoying the beautiful sights. The people who made this game clearly did so with a passion. The soundtrack often matches perfectly with the vibe of the world. The character's facial expressions are animated wonderfully, and they are all impactful to have around. 

All my complaints are minor, and I still plan to go through the new game+ soon. Great game.

The atmosphere, the music, the world design, the characters, the gameplay systems, everything matters to me.

Because of that, it is honestly very difficult for a game to completely surprise me and make me fall in love with it.

But Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 did exactly that.

I never expected a game to surpass some of my personal favorites like Assassin's Creed 2 or Life is Strange. Those games always had a special place for me. But this game changed everything.

I started this game with a lot of doubts.

On paper nothing about this game would be something I would enjoy. I do not care for turn based combat, I do not get too bogged down in story or lore, and I never get emotionally invested in characters or really identify with them. If story and characters do resonate with me in a game, then that is awesome and I am here for it. However, normally I am a combat-driven game mechanics type of player and that is really the only thing that matters to me. The hype and energy around this game was so unreal that, against my better judgement, I decided to try it out despite those things. I am so happy to say that this game proved me incredibly wrong on all of those things as Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took me on one of the most fun, intense, and emotional rides in a video game I have ever had.

Gameplay

Right off the bat this game solves my main gripe with turn based combat. You actually get to participate during your opponents turns through the parry and dodge mechanics. No more waiting around to play the game again, or hoping for favorable RNG if you were to get hit. You now get to time dodges or parry attacks when it is your opponents turn, and based on how well you do those two things you can generate more action points (AP) for when it is your next active turn to do more special attacks. This is such a welcome addition that I hope other turn based combat games adopt this model. If Expedition 33 is not the first then chalk this statement up to me not having played enough of them. 

All player characters have a unique fighting style which gives each of them their own subsystems that you will need to learn, but the game does a good job explaining them and they do become intuitive. There are six player characters in total so you end up with two teams of 3. One being Team A and the other being Team B which comes out in the event that your main three fall. Due to each character having their unique combat styles and there being six of them, the leveling and customizing loadouts can be a bit overwhelming as you have a lot to keep up with. Not only are you leveling your character stats and weapons which synergize with each other in terms of scaling, but you are also keeping up with your pictos and lumina abilities which you can think of these as character perks. These are perks such as: gain a shield when falling below 50% health, or my favorite one, every parry generates an additional AP point. There are a ton of these to sort through and make a judgement call on who should get which perk. The good news is, basically every build in this game works well so even if you just throw some perks haphazardly to your characters and do not optimize them, you can still absolutely do well in this game.

Graphics & Art Direction

Expedition 33 is stunning from both fidelity and art direction perspectives. On one hand the game packs a major punch when it comes to resolution and detail of the world, characters, and enemies. Then on the other hand it has the most unique environments and enemy/boss designs as far back as I can remember. When I was playing the game there never came a time when pattern recognition kicked in and I could draw a comparison between what I experienced in Expedition 33 and any other game I played previously. Clair Obscur is undeniably its own thing. The use of various color pallets is on a very high level of eye candy. The colors are punchy, vibrant, and bold. Environments will range from bright & upbeat to somber & depressed that fit the story seamlessly. The latter are even with pops of color that give such nice contrast to the darks that I think OLED monitor owners will be very pleased.

Story

I am not going to regurgitate the synopsis you can find anywhere online. I am going to be very brief overall as you simply just need to experience it for yourself. I do not want to risk ruining or detracting from your experience somehow. Just know this, there are no cheap tricks used to pull at your heartstrings, and everything gets the proper time to marinate and develop before you are explicitly explained anything. Even if you are very good at piecing stories together and you predict most things, you will still be happy with this one. The voice acting is phenomenal, the music is beautiful, hauntingly beautiful at that, and the writing is top notch.

Most overrated game in a while. Story has a good setup, but becomes awful the longer you play, most characters literally becoming meaningless, the dialogues are absolutely boring and the game pulls some of the worst cliches in fiction. The gameplay is fun at first, but gets worse the longer you play as well, it becomes a rhythm game devoid of any real strategy.

[h1]"For those that come after"[/h1] 
I've never seen a game undermine it's main theme so heavily by claiming to be looking forward to a brighter future whilst the story and it's characters are obsessively stagnating in the past. 

There is also no character development at all really, each character is the same as they were when they started. They never really look at their grief or loss any different than when it all started. At best they exchange witty banter every once in awhile and might share "dark secrets" of their past. 

That is not even mentioning the pace of the game, most of the story takes places at the beginning and end of each Act. So there are large gaps where they are hoping vague information will be enough to carry you forward through the story. With the 3rd Act giving you almost too much information to the point it makes it hard even want to progress to the end because the motivations moving the plot forward come off childish and makes the story feel like unnecessary padding.

[h1]Combat[/h1]

I get why people like the combat but feels at odds with itself as well. There is a awesome and tight strategy system here but the bosses never really ask you to deviate and it can be easily undermined by the action combat that comes during the opponents turn by parrying well. These action elements feel too strong and aren't situational enough to be that interesting. Sure, the timing changes but the mobs in the area also clue you in on the sort of timings and moves you will be dealing with so by the time you're at the boss you're not really learning all that much. I just wish there was more incentive to change my play and that the opponent's turn didn't take focus over the strategic elements of the player turn as it feels like what you do during the opponent's turn matter so much more.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]

[h2]Music[/h2]

 The soundtrack for this game is amazing. Ranging from electronic drum beats to grand operatic orchestrations. I would definitely recommend giving the soundtrack a listen. I would be shocked if there is not at least one track you enjoy.
 
[h2]Visuals[/h2]

The visuals in this game are nothing short of stunning. The atmosphere is pitch perfect, the enemy designs are visual unique from anything I've seen and honestly genuinely lack comparison as they truly feel original short of a few areas like a water themed area where the enemies have anchors or underwater mines but that is about. The environments are filled with cool little visual elements even with it being small instanced environments. I would not fault you taking a screenshot from this game and slapping it as your background.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

The experience did not feel cohesive and there are some really cool ideas there to be sure so I can understand how some people can enjoy this game but I can't personally recommend it as the sum of it's part did not work for me personally. However, if you feel you can overlook it's flaws and embrace the canvas then I would say go for it.

[h3]For Those Who Come After[/h3]

[b]Clair Obscur: Expedition 33[/b] is one of those rare games where logic and nonsense coexist perfectly. It’s dark-fantasy with a human heart, where characters actually talk and feel like people. Every dialogue, every pause, every breath matters. And that soundtrack - melancholic, jazzy, with a touch of saxophone - when was the last time you heard something like that in a video game? I’m sure it’s going to get an award at [b]The Game Awards[/b]. It deserves one. (i'm absolutely sure that game will win GOTY award).

The engine is insane, and so is the combat. It’s a mix of tactical rhythm and action, something close to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, yet completely its own thing. After beating the first Mime, I realized just how precisely the system is tuned - it rewards focus, timing, and understanding of your enemies. And if you’re looking for a real challenge - Expert mode is waiting for you.

The world design itself feels both chaotic and deliberate. Locations look intimidating at first, but they all loop back in subtle ways - circular routes, shortcuts, hidden areas, side bosses. It’s simple, rewarding, and fun to explore, especially during the first 2/3 of the game. I spent about an hour just wandering through the first city, and it felt alive - detailed, artistic, and surprisingly huge for a game of this budget. The art direction and scale are way beyond what you’d expect from an indie project. It even carries a bit of that LucasArts/Double Fine humor, hidden under layers of darkness and melancholy.

Exploration is more than just traversal; it’s a form of archaeology. In the middle of Act I, I started taking notes about locked paths and unfinished encounters - it genuinely felt like being part of an expedition. The voice journals - one per fallen expedition - are the best use of recorded lore I’ve seen in years. They make the world feel old, tragic, but still human.

By the end of Act II, after over sixty hours of play, I still had about half of the hidden achievements locked. That says everything about the game’s depth. The boss fights are tough but fair - the main ones feel like challenges, the side ones feel like real trials. There are hard boss milestones, escalating in difficulty, showing you the limits of your skills if you choose to face them. And after long sessions of exploration and side content, returning to the main story feels like finally taking a deep breath.

Then there’s the writing. The moment that completely hooked me was a conversation with Mael in the prologue. Someone mentioned earlier that she’s sixteen. At the end of the prologue, Gustave asks her why she wants to join Expedition 33, and she replies:

[h1]“It’s better to go with you for one year than spend nine years here.”[/h1]

That line hit hard. Because time moves in both directions in this world - it means her final Gommage will come when she’s twenty-three or twenty-four. That’s insane. Subtle, poetic storytelling that quietly destroys you.

This is a game with the look of a AAA blockbuster and the soul of an indie. It’s brutal like Dark Souls, dreamlike like Ori, and emotional like the best story-driven adventures. It’s a world where common sense triumphs over death, yet every character remains tender, warm, alive, and deeply compassionate.

If Unreal Engine 5 allowed small team to create project like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, then it’s one of the best things that could happen to the gaming industry.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 starts off with one of the most gripping openings to a game I’ve ever experienced and only continues to ramp up from there. At its core, it tells a deeply emotional story of loss and grief in a beautifully realized, unique world.

The combat system for this turn based jrpg takes familiar elements from different games, both classic and new, and combines them into an addictive system. The addition of dodging and parrying keeps you constantly on your toes. Learning enemy attack patterns to execute the perfect counter is immensely satisfying. At the moment, I can’t imagine there being another jrpg as engaging as this game.

The game oozes confidence with every passing frame. From the music and world building to the progression system, enemy designs, voice acting, and dialogue, all exceptionally good. Knowing that this is coming from a small studio of largely inexperienced developers makes it all the more remarkable.

The only negative experience I had was related to pacing around the middle of the game. In that instance, the game felt a bit bloated and repetitive. However, this is a minor gripe in an otherwise incredibly well rounded, fun game.

This game has easily cemented its position among my favorite games of all time.

As a final piece of advice, do yourself a favor and go into it knowing as little as possible to get the absolute best experience.

I would never have thought I would enjoy a turn-based game but this one captured me and spit me out 90 hrs later questioning where else can I get another game engaging to its extent. With all the QTs and parries I didn't have a glimmer of boredom I usually get while playing TBGs.

The way Clair-Obscur (chiaroscuro) is both the key for the visuals and a metaphor for its narrative is just delightful. So many people I know told me this game brought them joy, so I really did want to like this and share that with them. But I just don't. I tried my best to temper my expectations for this game after it swept TGA last year. I was sure it would be at least good, regardless of how overhyped it may or may not be. I was determined to give it a fair shot. And yet, I simply could not bring myself to enjoy Expedition 33.

It's not an awful game by any means and there are plenty of positives. Narratively it's mostly fine, it's a story about grief, how it blinds us, the trials and tribulations it brings and the lengths people go to avoid confronting reality, that sort of thing. The actual execution of it is nothing I would sing praises to the heavens for but I think it's okay, the idea is good, even with the clumsy pacing and sometimes strangely written dialogue. The music is also great, I found myself humming the main Lumière motif while doing chores. The voice actors also did a great job, Jennifer English in particular is standout and Andy Serkis is great as usual. If this had been a film or series it'd be pretty good.

But for me that's about as far as the positives go. For the rest of it, I really, [i]really[/i] do not see what people find so compelling about it. I think Team Cherry (Hollow Knight devs) summed it up best when they described it as "broadly palatable." 

My biggest grievance by far is with combat. Dodging was fine, although the parry timing felt really strange to get used to even with the clear audio cues. But the window/timing of them wasn't my issue with it. I think dodges and parries [i]can[/i] work in a turn-based system, but in this game I simply do not think it works at all. For me, the critical issues are:
[list]
    [*]For a turn-based system, it relies so heavily on its parry mechanic that it becomes absurd. I [i]really[/i] don't care if the counterattack animation is full of aura farming and bass boosted sound effects. In turn based systems, the rewarding feeling comes from putting together a team of character builds and carrying out your strategy successfully. In Expedition 33, that rewarding feeling for your stat choices, skill combinations, speed tuning, etc, all goes out the window because the reward so heavily hinges on long chains of parrying. Dodges also seem to exist mostly just to feel out an enemy's attack pattern, after which you are absolutely expected to parry everything. Your builds and strategies mean nothing if you do not master the parry system. There's even Verso's entire gameplay loop actively punishing you for missing a dodge or parry by lowering his rank and therefore his damage. Adding a real-time mechanic to a turn-based system, and then only rewarding players for mastering the former, is an atrocious design choice.
    [*]Dodges and parries do not deliver anything close to the same sense of satisfaction and skill improvement as they do in a real-time ARPG (i.e. the genre they come from) because there's no movement. I don't have the same options of, say, dodging in a specific direction to position myself for a better attack window, or creating some distance so I have space to heal, or blocking an attack with a shield if I don't want to reposition with a dodge, or anything in that vein of thinking. It is entirely a matter of pressing RB with the correct timing several times in a row, ad infinitum. It isn't fun. Having it as a limited option as part of a wider toolset would be one thing, and I'd be interested to see a different turn-based game try to pull that off, but in this game it's seemingly the very foundation of combat itself. Given it has a rather good soundtrack, combat might as well have just been a rhythm game instead. I don't want to call it "parryslop" but it's becoming more and more difficult to resist doing so.
    [*]In addition to the QTE-like nature of parries, there are also literal QTEs whenever you take a turn. You press the A button a couple of times when prompted. It's always the A button. It's not fun or satisfying and adds nothing to the experience. There's even an option in the settings to just automatically have these QTEs succeed... why even bother having these?
[/list]

Another big point of praise this game receives is its visuals and graphics. I can see what they were going for narratively with a painted world, but so much of it was just utterly mediocre in every sense of the word. Visual flair comes entirely from Unreal Engine's raytracing and bloom filter. I don't have a raytracing GPU so the whole "wow cool graphics" song and dance was lost on me and the game looked like ♥♥♥♥, and I'm not exactly in a rush to upgrade with the currently ♥♥♥♥♥♥ market for components thanks to the AI bubble. Speaking of which, I really struggled to think of any other explanation for its world and level design than the devs saying "ChatGPT generate concept art for a beautiful painted world" and going from there. Places where the ground was covered in snow yet random patches of nothing were on fire, train tracks clipping through a brick wall as if the model was placed there on a whim and the dev said "job done," and many more such instances.

The art direction consists mostly of oversaturated colours vomited all over the place. (I know [i]why[/i] it's like that, I just think it's poorly done.) The level design seems to consist of random asset store items floating in midair with an equally random grappling hook mechanic connecting them. The parry sound effect sounds like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ vine boom. So much of this game is painfully mediocre. Things like animation quality or enemy balancing can easily be dismissed as this being the studio's debut project, but most things cannot.

Far from unique to this game but it's also horribly optimised. I was averaging 40-50 fps at 1080p for most of the game while on the [i]lowest possible[/i] graphics settings (including XeSS Ultra Performance with resolution scale 33.3%). I know Sandfall is a new indie studio and this is their debut project, but if I can play certain recent AAA games on low-medium settings at a stable 60fps at 1080p without any upscaling, then I really don't think this is reasonable. (That said, it may not be Sandfall's fault, Unreal Engine is a plague.)

Also, although the story is mostly fine, I think the forced moral choice at the end was really stupid. The game is very clearly opinionated on the moral choice in question (which is good! writers should be opinionated!) but then presents you with a choice to say "thats crazy bro" and contradict the entire point of the story in the first place, and changes the philosophy of discussion around it from grief and escapism and confronting reality, which is interesting, into [spoiler]are the painted people real humans[/spoiler], which is the sort of boring nonsense you'd see in 2hr slop video essays on game lore. Really strange writing decision. Why go to such lengths to set up the moral dilemma only to ruin it?

It's an impressive debut project for a studio of Sandfall's size, while also being a [i]monumentally[/i] overrated game. Both can be true at the same time.
