[h2] Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took the Turn-Based genre into the next level with its remarkable real-time mechanics, offering the freedom to explore both its rich world and enhancing each character builds. [/h2]  
[h2] Writing & Plot [/h2]
The narrative is set in an aesthetic and artistic dark fantasy world inspired by the Belle Époque period of France, creating a unique dreamlike world. Every year, a mysterious entity known as the Paintress awakens to paint a number on a monolith, and everyone of that age fades away. Each year, this number decreases, leading to a desperate mission commissioned to end the cycle before the next number is written. Expedition 33 embarks on this perilous journey like those before them to save future generations of Lumiere, an isolated city on an island in the ocean. Our heroes, Gustave, Maelle, Lune, and Sciel, find themselves in crisis after an unexpected encounter that led to the annihilation of most of their members upon reaching the shore of the continent where the Paintress resides. However, new friendly creatures join them on their adventure to destroy the Paintress. 

Initially, the story appears to be about survival, but as you delve deeper, it reveals itself to be something entirely different. It emerges as a portrayal of grief, and once that realization hits, everything changes. Even the ending you choose doesn’t deliver a simple closure; instead, it mirrors the various ways we cope with loss. It’s beautiful and poetic in its own right. The characters you once viewed as antagonists reveal themselves to be humans trying to mend broken bonds. No ending is inherently right or wrong, so feel free to choose the one that resonates with you the most. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3710138113
[h2] Character Building [/h2]
The character building and writing work hand in hand to reinforce the game’s emotional core. Each character distinctly responds to grief, conveyed not through dialogue but through subtle visual details and restrained performances. Rather than relying on heavy exposition, the game lets small gestures define who these people are.

What truly adds depth to the narrative is how the game handles its character bonds. Their relationships aren’t just supportive, but they are complex and realistic. They are deepened by the shared burden of not only saving Lumière but also coping with loss and despair. 
[h2] Aesthetics & visuals [/h2]
The art direction and world design are unrivaled, bringing to life a vivid reality out of a canvas. As you embark on your adventure through these beautifully crafted realms, you can't help but be enchanted by the breathtaking landscapes and sense their sheer beauty. Not only do these stunning views catch your attention, but also the meticulously composed music that elevates your gaming moments into a one-of-a-kind experience that lingers in your memory long after you've explored every corner. It's truly an unforgettable exploration of beauty and creativity.

One area that truly captivates the attention is Sacred River, a mystical and serene realm where creatures await their rebirth. In this enchanting landscape, a dazzling aurora waves across the night sky. Its vibrant hues of green and blue paint a magical portrait along the stars. Enormous glowing bells suspended midair cast a gentle, soft blue light that illuminates the land in an otherworldly glow. The environment is abundant with life, yet it leaves you with a sense of lost memories of each reborn creature. There are trees and crystal-clear water that flow through the land, reflecting the beauty of the moon high above, surrounded by the glow of the bells.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3710133457
[h2] Gameplay Mechanics [/h2]
The gameplay combines the traditional turn-based RPG combat system with unique real-time mechanics, making each encounter dynamic. In battle, players can utilize free aim, parrying, and dodging, which are crucial skills to master. Specifically, the parry and gradient counter can inflict significant damage if executed with perfect timing. Additionally, players can earn extra XP if they avoid taking any hits.   

The game also offers the freedom to strategize your battles and builds. Each character possesses unique abilities, skill trees, and synergies. Pictos are tools that increase the character's stats and grant various effects, such as boosting attacks and defenses, as well as conditional effects, for instance, dealing more damage to the enemy at the cost of doubling the damage the character receives. Each character can equip up to three pictos, making the selection process a strategic decision. Luminas are passive abilities that can be activated once you fully master a picto without equipping it to a character. This feature allows you to customize your build to fit your playstyle by improving your stats, skills, and gear.

Outside of combat, the game features open-world exploration. Players can adventure through the world by going on foot or travel with their giant companion by swimming and flying to discover hidden paths, battle bosses, engage in side quests, mini-games, collect materials for upgrades, hunt for collectibles, and interact with party members to deepen the connection and get new skills as a reward. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3696599627
[h2] Conclusion & Final Thoughts [/h2]
I could analyze every character, area, and event, and connect them to various layers and themes; yet, I would still feel that I hadn't explored enough. It's a mesmerizing tale, perfectly executed, and I am in awe of the countless details the developers, writers, and composers worked so hard to create. The soundtrack is rich in lyrics, and it is one of the elements that initially drew me in because they convey the characters' emotions and hardship. Overall, it features a strong and profound narrative while enjoying its world.

I was hesitant to play it, but after finishing it, it became one of the best games of my life. Thank you to the development team for creating this masterpiece.

Look, I play every game in a way that makes most normal people rage-quit after the first hour. If I'm not pushing a game's mechanics to the absolute breaking point, I'm not having fun. So when I booted up Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 for the very first time, I immediately cranked it to the highest difficulty setting, stripped my party down to a single character, and committed to a parry-only run. No dodges, no safety nets.

What I didn't expect was for the game to actually hold up to that level of punishment—and completely destroy me emotionally at the same time.

The Story Actually Hooks You
I don't care how hardcore you think you are, the beginning of this game will make you tear up. Every single time I watch that opening cinematic, it hits me like a truck. Watching the Paintress wake up to paint that number on the monolith and just erase an entire generation of people into smoke is brutal.

From minute one, I was obsessed with figuring out what was going on. My head was spinning with the same three questions the whole time: Who the hell is the Paintress? Why is she doing this? What even is this place? The writing is so incredibly tight that it forces you to care. You aren't just grinding for stats; you genuinely need to know the truth behind the Gommage.

Taking the World Record
Because the combat in this game is so flawlessly tuned, you can pull off some absolutely unhinged stuff if you have the patience and the execution. And I have the patience.

Someone out there was sitting on the actual World Record for most perfect parries in a single boss fight with 10,000. I decided that wasn't going to fly. I sat at my desk for almost 8 straight hours against a single boss, completely locked in.

Here is the final breakdown of that fight:

Damage Taken: 0

Dodges: 0

Perfect Parries: 12,315

Taking the official World Record by perfectly deflecting over twelve thousand hits in a row without a single mistake is the wildest gaming experience of my life. My hands were completely dead by the end of those eight hours, but executing that flawless 1-character, parry-only run was worth it. Every single attack thrown at me, I just stood my ground and perfectly deflected it.

The Verdict
Expedition 33 isn't just a good RPG; it is the absolute peak of the genre. Whether you're here for an incredibly well-written story that will actually make you cry, or you're a complete masochist like me who wants to spend 8 hours perfectly timing blocks to steal a world record, buy this game right now.

10/10.

I'm in the minority here, I know, but I don't think this game was very "good". It’s frustrating and doesn’t respect your time or intelligence. It’s got great ideas, with mostly good execution, but can’t deliver on its many promises in a lot of key areas. Should you play this? Probably. Everybody else is doing it.

But I can’t recommend it. It’s a beautiful EXPERIENCE, but only a half-decent GAME.

Possible indirect spoilers ahead!

>VISUALS AND STYLE<
This thing is unbelievably gorgeous, richly detailed, and vivid in a way that defines this generation. No disagreement there. Creative beyond easy description. 20/10.

The voice acting, motion capture, and character animations are similarly excellent. Easily 10/10, putting BG3 or any other RPG to absolute shame.

>THE STORY<
Hit-or-miss. It’s hard to critique without spoilers, so please excuse the vagueness.

At times the story is brilliant and the storytelling both immersive and engaging. At other times, it feels like a draft from an earlier version of the game. There’s a hell of a lot of tonal whiplash going on. It feels VERY French. And I am usually fine with that, but there is something about how it’s presented as an interactive story that left me feeling unsatisfied.

Example: All those frenzied, bloody battles you win by the skin of your teeth early on gives way to a village of goofy creatures. Which is… okay. It gets explained later. But it doesn’t feel right.

The introduction of the main villain(s) isn’t handled very well. The trope of “you knew the whole time” is basically our entry point into the broader conflict. This is when you’ll start scratching your head and saying things like “wait, who?” and “I don’t understand”.

By midgame the worldbuilding transitions from organic storytelling and character interactions to very forced “we must go here because of this” quips. Things start going full anime, as the gods and monsters aspect of the world becomes the main focus. You spend more and more of your time being TOLD things instead of experiencing them.

You aren’t playing a cohesive experience anymore. You’re playing a visual novel with QTEs. But it keeps delivering... until Act III. Oh my God. What should have been a thrilling revelation lands like a dead fish. The whole thing becomes a soap opera! EXTREME EMOTIONS and PROPER NOUNS, without breathing room or context! ANGST and CRISIS!

After some waffling, the story gives up and dumps you back into the world to kind of wander around and do content. No more narrative leading you from place to place. No more story reveals. Just a bunch of map locations of varying interest.

You have to make your own story here, at tremendous expense of your time. Act III’s story is mostly locked behind BRUTAL boss encounters and high level enemies. It sucks. (see below)

And then, all of a sudden, the game abandons the agency of your characters. Who cares what they want or why? They’re just pushed aside in favor of the gods and monsters plot, never to be heard from again.

The endings had me yelling at the screen. “I DON’T UNDERSTAND WHAT CHOICES I AM MAKING HERE!”

But it doesn’t matter, because the choices are binary, absolute, astoundingly brief (30 second movie clips), and deeply unsatisfying. Was that a wink to the audience? A subtle acknowledgement of the horror of existence and the continuation of a cycle of abuse? Who the hell knows?

This is that French thing again, a pervasive notion of nihilism that runs through the story, where nothing seems to actually matter. The whole first half of the game proudly says “we must save our world”, while the second half slowly smokes its cigarette and asks “but what’s the point?”.

>THE GAMEPLAY<
I can forgive absolutely everything above, but the core gameplay loop sucks. I feel bad saying this.

I think the developers said something like "dodge and parry are optional" which is absolutely NOT the case. Hope you’re up for a soulslike/fighting game level timed button pressing experience!

The idea of a turn-based soulslike *sounds* good on paper, but in practice it is a SLOG. Every battle seems to devolve into punishing, multi-part attacks requiring precision timing to survive, even at high levels. Your basic mobs can use you as toilet paper if you don’t dodge one of six different attacks per turn. Is this fun?

There’s some kind of timing issue here I could NEVER break into. I usually do very well in action games and action RPGs. I understand that the audio is a clue to when to push buttons. Sometimes I could close my eyes and nail the timing. But I could not, after 30+ hours, reliably time my reactions to the enemy attacks. So all that preparation, leveling, picto assignment, weapon upgrading, etc. was meaningless. A level 99 party against a level 50 enemy can still get smeared by missing one or two attacks.

Boss battles are awful. Every one of them has brutal multi-part attacks, multi-part turns, and screw-you mechanics. Make sure you’re ready to dodge 18 attacks, three times in a row, for twenty minutes as your party gently sands down the boss’ HP meter. Is this fun? I don’t think so. Get ready to die a lot in pursuit of enemy attack timing and strategy. I get that, it’s a soulslike.

But when presented as a turn based RPG, it feels like failure. There is some messaging here that is not quite right when the “FAILED” message pops up. Regular battles restart quickly, but boss battles kick you back out into a cutscene (which you can skip), that makes it feel like you were NOT supposed to die.

And holy hell, this gets more and more pronounced in act III. The only thing the game has left to throw at you are massive HP bars and multi-hit attacks. Dodge, parry, occasionally deliver a limp slap of your own. If this is your thing, great. The late game rewards this and is built around it. But it was jarring and miserable for me.

I conducted an experiment, I turned off the action camera in battle to see if a locked camera would improve my dodge and parry rate improved.  This stops the camera from dropping behind your character during an attack, etc. as a motion sickness prevention option.

That made a HUGE difference. Being able to see the whole enemy instead of just a front 3/4 view helped with my timing, even with many enemy attacks obscured by the player characters or occuring partially offscreen. I think it improved my success rate by 50% or more.

This is a problem. The camera isn’t showing the enemy attack in a way that allows visual clues to be quickly identified and reacted to. And the enemy attacks are staggered, jittery, halting, and often misdirect you into missing the impact. This is creative and adds natural difficulty, but it screws up the timing! Feel free to point out that I suck. I probably do. But the dodge and parry mechanic is THE MOST IMPORTANT part of the game. The RPG side is kind of an afterthought.

I haven’t even mentioned the upgrade system or the abilities, because they don’t make that much of a difference overall. Weapon leveling is unguided, and you can waste a lot of VERY hard to find resources leveling the wrong weapon, which screws you for almost the whole game. Hope you didn’t spend ALL those upgrade items on the wrong weapon! Because your stats are tied to them! 

HP, speed, defense, etc. are assigned by points, but depend entirely on your weapon level or equipped pictos (ability items) to be meaningful. It’s not BAD, but it’s criminally under-explained and by the time you figure out what’s going wrong, you’ve been struggling against enemies for hours.

It is PUNSHING. It wastes your time. It throws variety at you, but overwhelms you with unguided choices. Without an online guide, you’ll be lost and frustrated. 

Is that fun? I don’t think so.

I didn't know what to expect with this game before playing it. I barely knew anything about it before it won 9 awards at The Game Awards and honestly, I'm really glad I didn't know anything. I've been playing video games for over 75% of my life. It's almost impossible for me to remember a time in my life where I wasn't playing video games. I have never been more reminded of why I fell in love with playing games than while I was playing this one. It reminded me why video games are a medium. Why video games are an art. Why I and millions of other people come home everyday to play video games instead of engaging with the outside world.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is an experience like no other. It's something you have to play at least once in your lifetime, because there isn't another game out there that will give you the experience that this game gives you. Everything about this game, the story, the characters, the world, the art, the battles, and goodness that soundtrack is the best thing I've ever heard out of a video game. It all feels so well crafted to the point of near perfection that you may start to think that the developers were visited by a higher power at some point in its creation. I don't want to say that much specifically about the details of this game because I feel it might take from your own experience if you go and play it. All I can say is, just try it once. You will smile, you will laugh, you will cry, and your eyes better be glued to the pixels that are being projected from your monitor. This game may be fiction, but it'll make you feel like it's real. I wouldn't say Clair Obscur is a bad game but it didn't click with me; I think it's not a game for everyone. I wasn't much of a fan of the very corridor like areas, the animations or some parts of the UI, but what I really disliked was the combat.

What you have to know about combat is that it's a classic turn based jrpg combat style in the line of games like the FF1-9 era, which is fine, but with a twist : You can evade or better, parry attacks. This mechanic was (for me) both not enjoyable and a bad design decision. if you get the timing right, parrying means that you take no damage at all and also retaliate for massive amount of damage.
Having to perform QTEs on both attack and defense is very much not my thing, and that can be worse if you're bad at it, and it's a complete mess of balance because your build, your gear becomes irrelevant. Yeah maybe the fight will take a bit more time if you got no gear and crap build but as long as you can't take damage who cares right ?
Not only the parry/evade mechanic is broken, but it's kind of mandatory too because it's very likely you won't be able to outright tank some enemies, even on easy mode, so you HAVE to engage with this system.

I played up to the level 20 or so, and up to that point I didn't need to learn a single spell, didn't rank a single stat and barely interacted with the passive system; my characters were just straight out of the box so to say. I just parryed my way to victory... This made the game very boring to me, and after 6 hours I was forcing myself to play so I gave up.

So I'm not gonna sit here and pretend this game reinvented storytelling like some people claim. 
I've played enough RPGs, especially turn based ones to know this level of passion and writing has existed for decades. 
Early Final Fantasy, Xenoblade, you name it. But hey, ex Ubisoft devs, cool backstory, pretty trailers...I get why people were surprised.
The premise itself is gorgeous. 
The world feels unique and the characters? 
Man, the voice acting is insane! 
Some of the best I've heard in a game. They carry half the emotional weight just by talking. 
The praise is understandable but on Steam, at least, it's blown way out of proportion. 
Some basic achievements sit at 25-30% completion which tells me a lot of people played a bit, got sick of the gameplay, refused to admit it, watched streamers fake tears for views and suddenly it's "best game ever." 

- I'll start with the negatives first:
- Now...Unreal Engine. A blessing from far away, a curse up close. The vistas look amazing, no doubt but the moment you zoom in, characters sometimes look too sharp and the movement feels floaty. Unreal Engine has this eternal struggle with "weight" so you end up controlling characters that feel like they're gliding through a museum. Beautiful museum, sure but you can't touch anything.

- Gameplay though...yeah, here's where the game loses me. 
I get what they were trying to do: "Let's spice up turn based combat!" 
Cool idea. In theory.

In practice? Welcome to 
"Parry Souls: Turn Based Edition."
The whole combat system revolves around pressing a button at the right time. 
Not a dodge, not a chance, not a stat, not a build. It's just you pressing the same button over and over and if you don't master it? 
Good luck. The game will slap you around until you do.
The game starts off pretending it's not 100% timing based and then it reveals that yes, actually, it is. Completely. Every enemy, every boss, every random dude with a stick. 
Learn their pattern or suffer.
Parry gives you more action points and a big counter at the end of the turn. 
Miss one parry? 
Counter gone. 
So you dodge instead. 
But then you lose the bonus. 
So you parry. 
But then you get hit. 
So you dodge. 
And suddenly you're not playing a turn based RPG anymore.
You're playing a rhythm game with swords.
And look, I can parry. I can dodge. I can learn patterns. That's not the issue. 
The issue is that this system becomes the entire personality of the game. 
It's like adding a second button to a shooter so every bullet you fire needs "extra confirmation" to deal full damage. 
Or in a racing game, you press accelerate and then another button to "really" accelerate pops up.
It slows things down after a while, takes away from the spectacle of the game and 20 hours in, you'll be sick of it. It gets frustrating fast and dying to a boss because you didn't press a button at the right millisecond? 
Yeah, that's not fun.
Some enemies have so much HP that you'll end up spending hours (including failed attempts) trying to kill them. 
It doesn't respect your time and of course, later they add even more timing buttons, because why not...

- The pictos are cool, I'll give them that. 
They change fights and add variety but the community obsession with "you didn't build correctly" or "use this combo" or "stack this stance" kills the fun. 
If I have to leave the game and google "1 hit builds" just to make the game enjoyable, that's not good design. 
I'm not playing a story driven RPG so I can talk to strangers online about how to deal billions of damage by stacking elements. The game should give players more accessible tools by default.

- It honestly feels like most of the teams behind this game went all in and aimed for a huge impact and in many areas they actually pulled it off. 
But because of how the gameplay is designed, the whole thing falls apart the moment you start exploring "too well." 
By the end of the game, I decided to explore everything. I mastered the parry/dodge timing, I learned the patterns and I was able to beat bosses way above my level because the game basically lets you break it if you're stubborn enough. 
The consequence of that? 
I walked into the final story area and the final boss died in four minutes. 
Four. 
I didn't even get to see what attacks it had, what dialogue it said, nothing. 
That's not good game design...The challenge was gone, the payoff was gone and the "big moment" felt like a joke. 
When a game lets you deal millions of damage because the systems are so unbalanced, that's not depth, and it's not balancing. A game like this needs at least some controlled environment, some limits, something to keep the experience consistent. 
This one doesn't have it and it shows.

- The journal entries are a missed opportunity. 
Some are interesting but most feel goofy or too casual. 
They don't capture the desperation, sacrifice, or seriousness of the expeditions. 
They should've made you feel how close Expedition 34 was, how much 35 pushed, how much the others suffered. Instead, many entries feel random and some things don't make sense. 
Why would Expedition 60 discover something crucial when the path was only reachable thanks to the most recent expeditions? 
It would've made more sense for revelations to get stronger the closer we got to 33....
Whatever...

+ Now the positives because there are plenty. I won't go into too much detail but there's a lot of quality all across the board
+The story is phenomenal... 
Complex, unpredictable, emotional. 
You can tell the writers were fully invested and brought their absolute best. This is a really unique story in general. 

+The characters are memorable and well written and even the ones I didn't care about at first grew on me. 

+The voice acting is insane, some of the best I've heard. 
They carry half the emotional weight just by talking.

+ The music guy didn't have to go this hard but he did. 
Every area has its own track and some of them never repeat. 
It's crazy how good they are. 

+ The atmosphere, music and visuals dance together perfectly. 

It genuinely feels like different teams worked separately and gave their absolute best. 
Most of them crossed the finish line with flying colors. 
Only the gameplay team fell short for me. 
The story, characters, voice acting, music and world don't just carry the game but elevate it to greater hights... 
They even lift the combat higher than it deserves to be.

All in all, my rating has to be split. 
Visuals and world: 10/10. 
Characters: 10/10. 
Story: 10/10. 
Gameplay: 6/10.

Well, I can't believe I'm actually playing this game because I've largely put it off due to the crazy amount of hype and bandwagon-ing surrounding it, but 10 hours into the expedition I do have to say, the game managed to deliver my expectations and some. I don't know if I would necessarily rank E33 along the all-time greatest titles, but it definitely shows that it is made with love and care, something that is exceedingly rare in today's gaming market.

The game has absolutely phenomenal visual presentation, and supports the ultrawide format natively. I've ran the game on both 4K 32" and 1440p 34" ultrawide, and in both instances the game looks beautiful but for this kind of story-driven adventure, I do personally prefer the ultrawide form factor for its immersion. There was only one time where the game had a very brief black boxes around the sides during Maelle's Nightmare, but otherwise so far everything ran natively 21:9 no issues.

As someone who hated games that every single person talks about over and over, and being a rather harsh critic having grown up on titles like Chrono Trigger, Skyrim, Diablo, Warcraft and other all-time classics, E33 did manage to win me over. Whether it be the art direction, soundtrack, character design, storytelling or combat, it passes everything I have hoped that it would given its reputation. 

The operatic soundtrack sets the tone immediately and the amount of variation played on the main motif is refreshing and artistically delivered. In E33, music is not only integral to the experience but builds upon the narrative being driven, adding suspense, tenderness and other mixes of emotions during key moments of battle and story reveals. The pacing is very solid, there is just the right amount of storytelling mixed in with going through dungeons, and truly there's just never a dull moment unless you specifically choose to venture off into the wild and do the side content. The optional content gives nice outfits and weren't just entirely braindead "go fetch X item to Y" entirely, it feels like even the side NPCs serve some level of purpose instead of just being there for the sake of being there. 

I think most players will be pulled into the story 1-2 hours in and continue onwards seeking to find out more. This is exactly what happened to me and when a game manages to captivate, that's really all there needs to be said at the end of the day. I felt connected to the characters and shared their sense of hopelessness, dread, fear and desire to push on, it didn't feel like another cheap iteration of "random gang of nobodies goes out to fight big evil thing and save the world from certain doom" even though I do believe that's the idea so far, but perhaps I will have to revisit this point once I'm fully finished with the game. 

Just a quick final note for an initial impression, combat is very satisfying and I love that the game offers you rewards for playing well. If you learn the attacking patterns of enemies and can reliably parry/counter, you are able to take on enemies that if you were just playing a plain turn-based combat RPG you wouldn't be able to. Challenging the player to play well and rewarding them for it is an excellent approach to combat that I wish more games would adopt instead of just letting you grind mindlessly, get overlevelled and spam the A button to victory. You can do that too in E33, if you so wish, but that does take away the satisfaction of taking down a big baddie that you know you otherwise shouldn't have been able to if you didn't play very well and parried attacks on-point. The sound effects when you do land a counter also just gives such a nice dopamine hit, you love to see and hear it.

So far, there's really nothing negative I can pick out about E33 and I hope this will continue to be the case when I've completed my first run.

I am blown away by the massive amount of praise this game receives.
I think if you don't play many games (especially RPGs/JRPGs) this game could be the greatest game you ever play.
But every hour I slog (and it did quickly become a slog) through the game, the more the flaws in this gorgeous game became more and more glaring.

The Good:
The atmosphere, art, music, and voice acting are incredible.

The whole game is absolutely gorgeous, the environments feel like so much passion went into hand sculpting them, every little nook and cranny has set pieces that tell a story. The backgrounds and skyboxes are beautifully vibrant. The whole world is absolutely 10/10 one of the greastest works of art in video gaming.

The music is absolutely gorgeous constantly. It personally isn't my taste, I prefer more traditional video game music over orchestra, but that is a personal preference and the depth and effort is not lost on me.

The voice acting was immaculate, the actors elicited real emotion from me, both positive and negative, and I think they were all excellently chosen for their specific roles.


The Bad:

The UI forgoes user experience for artistic integrity, to the point that the game holds the visual theater experience higher than the gameplay experience of the user. 
The battle UI doesn't have good targeting markers, buff/debuff timers, and your character models can be over the top of the battle selections.
The in-combat camera cannot be manually moved, so enemy attacks and targeting can be difficult to see as the camera randomly decides to swing into your character's ankles and completely obscure your screen.

The status/equipment window out of combat is absolutely unacceptably abysmal. In lieu of making an interface that is user friendly and convenient, the game instead once again chooses aesthetics over usability.
Instead of a parsesable equipment and skills screen, you get a huge list that you can apply pre-set search terms. Which characters are in your party, or currently selected, or not in party, is denoted by a slightly different opacity of grey. Just use a damn highlight or arrow!

As well, when using any item or skill/buff on a character in your party in combat, there is almost zero indicator as to whom you are currently targeting besides the camera slightly panning towards them. A single arrow or highlight would have done wonders here. Just put a pointer next to the HP bars. This is industry standard.

The Ugly:

To me, gameplay and story are the primary draws to a game. Graphics and music are icing, but i'd rather eat a cake without icing than icing without cake.

1) The story:
______
I'm sorry to all the people that were blown away by the story of this game, I personally found it infuriatingly abysmal.
The prologue is the absolute peak, it was fantastic and set me up to expect an incredible story.
What follows that prologue is 20+ hours of every character speaking in prose, rhyme, riddle, and being generally as cryptic as possible to imply intrigue without actually advancing the story AT ALL.
Every dialogue with companions in the camp is as generic and uninteresting as reading a phonebook.
At ANY point in the story after chapter 1, the entire storyline would unravel if a single companion just said "What do you mean by that?" when any of the 20 important story characters says some cryptic poetic #deep line that every single cutscene boils down to.
The entire game sets you up for 20+ hours of asking yourself  "What is really going on? what does any of this mean? Why is the world like this?" to absolutely miss the mark spectacularly and undercut the entire premise it set up. I can't go into detail without spoilers, but unless you just don't read books or play RPGs or even watch a lot of cinema, I can't understand how this cliche riddled story feels anything more than a high schooler trying as hard as they can to be deep. A lot of the dialogue sounds like something Jaden Smith would have tweeted in 2019.

"This world isn't your world. This family isn't your family. This cycle isn't the cycle you should be trying to stop." 
-Jaden Smith NPC
"Uh.. What did he mean by that? Never mind, let's never mention it again" 
-Every character in my party.

If Expedition 33's story blew you away, I recommend the movie The Sixth Sense.
It has a better twist, respects your time by tying up the story in 2 hours, and doesn't masquerade as #deep with infuriatingly cryptic dialogue designed to manufacture intrigue.
If your story can't be interesting without hiding 95% of the details from the player for almost the entire game, the story wasn't interesting to begin with.
______

Combat:
This game took everything that made Final Fantasy 10 feel fantastic, and did it better.
Except instead of understanding why the UI was so convenient, they instead made it absolutely infuriating.
In every other RPG, in order to select a spell, you press down until you get to "Spell" and then click it and then click on the character you want to use it on.
In 33 you press Y then R2 then X then select your target based on the vague-ish direction of the camera then complete a QTE.
Every combat input for every turn in this game feels like i'm doing a Street Fighter combo to select a move.
Even after nearly 30 hours, I still have to think about which button combo gets me to the move I intend to use.
Use an item? X > Y > R2 > target > X
Use your break ability? Y > R2 > X > target > X
Mario RPG had this right 30 years ago.
Legitimately, Pokemon Red had better combat UI/UX.
But 33 just had to break the mold without understanding why that mold existed.

Parry/Dodge:
This is the mechanic that ruined the entire game for me.
On the medium and hard difficulties, the parry window is .15 seconds.
In Sekiro, Dark Souls, and Elden Ring, a parry has a .20 second window.
The parrying is harder in this game than soulsbourne games.
THIS IS AN RPG with FOUR DIFFERENT PARRY BUTTONS.
Each of which has different use cases, with different timing, which you will need to properly swap between, often 8+ times per attack per turn for each enemy later in the game. (Which often get multiple turns in a row)
And the parrying is BY FAR the most important action you will take in every single battle.
All your leveling, gearing, skill tree purchases, buffing, preparing, luminas, and pictos mean absolutely squat compared to your ability to properly QTE.
90% of this game's combat is resolved during your opponent's turn.
Every boss is a constant bombardment of QTEs with different timings, with no consistent tells, that will consistently try and fake you out with 6 second wind-ups, fake-outs, feints, and rapid fire combos.
The game teaches you early to use the audio cue, and then later many enemies do not have an audio cue, and then enemies attack BEFORE the cue or way after the cue.
Sometimes attacks slow down time, some don't, changing the parry timing.
Every single boss has to be memorized from fresh, every time.
What would have done this game a service, if they are married to the QTE parrying mechanic, is a rhythm game style response which is consistent so that you actually learn and get better at it as the game goes on.


The "classes":
33 decided standards be damned, we will break the mold again and go against the grain.
And by forgoing tropes such as a white mage, or cleric, every single character in 33 boils down to gameplay that feels like
"When you attack, gain a blim. When you have 4 blim points, you enter midnight stance. While in midnight stance, moves that cost blims instead cost blams but you take double damage and deal double damage, flip a coin to spin a wheel to see how many blams you get"

33 tries to break the mold by being intentionally different, but just ends up overcomplicating everything without improving it. Everything in the game: UI, story, classes, combat... feels intentionally contrived to appear deep, without improving on the basics they overcomplicated.

I have spent many hours with this game, yet I still struggle to understand its appeal as a Game of the Year.

The game’s insistence on mandatory parrying and dodging strikes me as fundamentally misguided. I fail to see the value in forcing reflex-based QTEs to become the decisive mechanic of what is ostensibly a turn-based RPG. The idea that success or failure hinges on perfectly timed button prompts feels not only awkward, but conceptually incoherent.

If what I seek is the excitement of QTE-driven combat, I can simply turn to an action game. At least in an ACT title, players are granted broader freedom of movement, greater tactical flexibility, and far more immediate and satisfying feedback. By comparison, compressing such mechanics into a rigid turn-based framework only highlights their limitations rather than their strengths.

To me, the core combat design resembles a child’s game of rock-paper-scissors—predictable, binary, and overly dependent on momentary reactions rather than meaningful strategic decisions. When an action-oriented feedback system becomes the determining factor in a turn-based game, one has to ask: why not just play an action game instead?

This hybridization feels less like innovation and more like a forced compromise, one that satisfies neither players who enjoy the depth and deliberation of traditional turn-based RPGs, nor those who seek the fluid intensity of pure action combat.

As a native Chinese speaker, I must also acknowledge that my detachment from the game may partly stem from a cultural gap. Much of the narrative’s French-inspired romanticism, symbolism, and fairy-tale references are simply unfamiliar to me. Elements such as the brush-headed creatures and other folkloric motifs may resonate strongly with Western audiences who grew up with similar stories, but for players outside that cultural context, these references are difficult to fully appreciate or emotionally connect with.

This is not necessarily a flaw in the game itself, but it does mean that part of its charm—so readily apparent to European or North American players—fails to translate effectively for us. As a result, the narrative weight that might elevate the experience for others feels muted, which further contributes to my overall sense of detachment from the game.

It is peculiar that The Witcher 3 remains my favorite RPG. Despite sharing a European ambience, its portrayal of the medieval world fills me with awe and fascination, and the game's extraordinary narratives and multifaceted world continue to linger in my thoughts. Perhaps, as some have observed in the comments, my response is guided not by mere cultural gap but by a sincere aversion to the ostentation and heavy-handed richness of French artistic style.

Right off the bat, this game made a great impression on me. When I launched it and got past the initial logo screens, I heard The Music. No, not music – The Music. At that point, it was just an introduction to OST, but it immediately gave me a feeling that the journey I was starting would be epic, and that The Whole Soundtrack (8 hours long!) would be just… something else. When I checked settings, still soaking in The Music, I really considered what language I wanted to hear throughout the game. There is a choice between English and French dubbing, and though English might seem to be an obvious option for most – especially with names such as Andy Serkis on board – I can’t imagine experiencing this story in other language than French. Because, citing after Jack Ze Whipper, “it is the most French thing that has ever been frenched”. I found it out right at the beginning of the game, when one of the main characters was dressed in a marinière, trousers with braces and a neckerchief, another important woman was wearing a stylish beret, there were boulangeries everywhere on my way, a creepy mime was ready to throw hands with me and above all, there was a weirdly twisted Eiffel Tower with 90 degrees scoliosis. I’m not even exaggerating. There were so many stereotypes thrown at me right of the get go that it was hard to believe this story would be serious. And yet within the next minutes, the rest of the prologue clearly showed me that yes – this whole ride was going to be very, very serious. Although, thankfully, well balanced with more light-hearted themes and dialogues.

It's incredible how much this game made me feel attached to a character that I only knew for a dozen or so minutes, and how artfully it played on my emotions with what happened during the prologue. It made me engaged in the whole story and lore immediately. And there is really a lot going on here. Everyone who read the description on the store page knows the initial premise about The Paintress who wakes up every year at the day of Gommage and erases all people older than the number on her Monolith, which gets lower by one every year. But this whole problem turns out to be much more complicated than this. When the player should theoretically reach the end of the story, it suddenly unfolds itself. It’s divided into three acts, and their endings bring some twists. One of them is quite gobsmacking, but admittedly, the game gave me enough hints to make me create multiple theories and actually lead me really close to guessing what the hell was going on. I read a book with a very similar plot point, so I kept it in mind as one of possible reveals here. Still, with the way it was presented, I was dumbfounded. The story is layered and complex, and whether someone likes it or not, one has to admit that it makes people think, analyse, consider various points of view – and then discuss.

Everyone has their own take on the endings we can choose here. None of them is good. Each “side” can explain their choice rationally based on their beliefs, worldview, experience with interpersonal dynamics and the way they interpret the whole conflict here. This game will be remembered and discussed for years to come – and for all the good reasons. Personally, I chose my ending based on my approach to grief. Because this game is all about it. Even The Paintress actually looses her mind out of grief. This is another reason why this story resonates with people so much – everyone was through this, everyone had to cope somehow, and can relate and lean towards certain arguments made by the characters.

Aside from the story, the artistic side is just as mesmerising. Locations are beautiful and unique and the enemies are well designed. I kept wandering and looking around before proceeding any further. I love exploring, and I lived my best life doing it here. Although the whole art style is great, the graphic has its flaws. There are weird artifacts around everyone’s hair and questionable default settings of sharpness and blur, and apparently most issues require some gymnastics in game files to get rid of them. I didn’t bother so much, though. I got used to the artifacts to the point I stopped seeing them, and they’re practically not visible on screenshots.

And once again, The Music… Seriously, many Hollywood blockbusters could be envious of this OST. There’s everything here – opera vocals, classical music, jazz, synth, rock-opera… Every new track was my instant new favourite, and when I thought I heard everything, I was hit by “Une vie à t’aimer” and got stun-locked for a minute or so. When I sprinted to check out the full version, I stumbled upon several shorts with streamers who were just as stunned as me. We were all there, guys. We can parry almost everything in this game, but we can’t parry The Music.

…and with the mention of parrying, let’s move swiftly to gameplay mechanics. Clair Obscur is a quite unusual hybrid of turn-based with real-time dodging and parrying to avoid damage. We have all the time in the world to plan next moves during our characters’ attack turn, but when the enemy attacks, we are expected to dodge or parry every hit by pressing a button at a very specific time. This general concept isn’t cutting-edge – it’s been around since the eighties. But it’s unusual enough to be many players’ first experience with this idea. It’s not everyone’s cup of tea, and people tend to either love or hate it. I really liked this system and learning the enemies’ attack timings. At first it’s easier to dodge, because the reaction window is more forgiving, but parrying is way more profitable. If you manage to parry all hits in a combo, you perform a powerful counter – and counters really turn the tables. Also, every single parry restores action points required to use skills.

Another vital part of the game are pictos and luminas. Pictos give various passive abilities and can be found through exploration or looted from enemies, and then equipped by one of the party members. After this character wins in four battles with said picto equipped, its ability is unlocked as a lumina. The difference is that a single picto can be used by only one person at the time, and each character can have three pictos at max. Luminas can be used by everyone at the same time, and there is no limit to how many luminas can a character use at the same time, but each has its own value in lumina points. Number of available points grow with levelling, and we can also use colours of lumina found through exploration and fights to increase the count. Both pictos and luminas can be changed at any given moments, so it’s very easy to shuffle the abilities so that the effects are suitable for various enemies. Also the attribute points can be easily rearranged, so the game encourages to try out different playstyles and synergies between abilities. Furthermore, all the effects from pictos and luminas stack, so it’s very easy to become absurdly powerful if you explore every nook and cranny and fight at least once with every enemy and manage to gather all available pictos this way. However, it works both ways – you can just as easily make your party much weaker by deactivating luminas.

There is a lot more that I would like to say, but it’s impossible without writing a book about this game, so I’d better wrap this review up. Clair Obscur is just a total package – complex and engaging story which touches mature themes and make people [i]think[/i], absolutely gorgeous OST, beautiful art direction and unusual gameplay mechanics. It’s not perfect, but it’s the strict top of the best games I have ever played. I really recommend everyone to give it a try.

I’ve seen so many online praising Expedition 33 as a work of art and absolutely deserving this year’s GOTY, but I honestly can’t agree.

First of all, Expedition 33 is an excellent game. The visuals, the Belle Époque–inspired art direction, and the music are all impressive. In terms of gameplay, it pushes the JRPG formula further (without the improved parry-counter and dodge system, it would’ve felt like another Persona 5 to me), but overall it’s still very solid.

However, the flaws in the story completely overshadow everything the game does well.

The opening of Expedition 33 is incredibly strong, the worldbuilding is captivating, the emotional setup is powerful, and the presentation is gorgeous. But when you reach the end, the game basically tells you that the dozens of hours you just spent fighting were meaningless — all your emotions, investment, and sacrifices were fake, just a painting.

It feels like the writers forced a twist just for the sake of having a twist. Everything the player believed they were doing — saving the world or making difficult sacrifices — turns out to be pointless. It’s like ending a story with, “I woke up, it was all just a dream,” or a Deus Ex Machina.

At its core, it’s narrative fraud — a violation of the narrative contract. The game starts by telling you, “The world is ending, and your efforts with the 33rd Expedition can save it.”
But the ending reveals [spoiler] “The world never existed.” [/spoiler]

It feels as if the writers couldn’t resolve the conflict they themselves created (couldn’t come up with a reasonable “save the world” ending), so they chose the cheapest solution,[spoiler] “None of it was real.” [/spoiler]By comparison, KCD2’s story may be cliché, but at least it fully honors its narrative contract (deliver the letter to another lord, face twists and turns, get dragged into new conflicts).

Some might say I just don’t appreciate the game’s nihilism or its philosophical exploration of death and existence.

But this reminds me of BioShock Infinite, which also explores death, existence, and philosophy. In that game, the protagonist even kills his past self, causing the entire story to “never have happened” within the game’s universe. Yet the journey still feels meaningful, and the ending fulfills the game’s opening promise “Bring us the girl, and wipe away the debt.”
BioShock Infinite achieves internal logical consistency and leaves players thinking deeply.

Expedition 33, on the other hand, feels more like emotional manipulation. My first reaction after finishing the story was “…That’s it?”
I wasn’t just disappointed — I was angry. It felt like wasted potential.

Many critics give Expedition 33’s ending high praise because it looks deep, blurs reality, or references philosophical ideas.

But to me, real depth is writing a compelling story within strict logical constraints (like KCD2’s historical realism), not flipping the table and saying[spoiler] “none of it was real.” [/spoiler]Anyone can flip the table — building something coherent on the table is the hard part.

Outside of the story, yes, KCD2 has bugs. But considering its extremely realistic and highly interactive open world, the flaws are forgivable, and the overall polish is clearly better than Expedition 33.

I’m not writing this to start a fight, I just want to express that while Expedition 33 is indeed an outstanding game, it doesn’t deserve GOTY.

This review contains no direct spoilers. It's nearly impossible for me to say why I don't like E33's story while being vague, but I'll try.

"I'm not angry, just disappointed." A quote from a character in E33 which happens to describe how I feel about the game.

Giving a negative review to a game that many consider "life-changing" and a "masterpiece" will probably make me seem contrarian for the sake of it. However, given the direction the story went and some of the more atrocious dialogue, I think E33 earned it, which is a shame because I thought for sure I'd love it. If you're thinking about buying it, I'd say be at least a little skeptical of the hype and consider whether or not the dialogue, the game's final act, and the ending all being "bad" could ruin the game for you before you do. If you expect a journey from E33, you'll probably get one, but a journey is remembered less fondly when the destination turns out to be ♥♥♥♥.

Starting with the obvious positives, E33 is extremely cinematic and well-presented, the environments are stunning, and the music is amazing. Given these things, it isn't hard to see why someone would call E33 a genuine masterpiece.

That said, I think this game deserves more criticism than it gets, particularly story/writing-wise. The boss Sirene feels like an unintentional representation of the game itself and how people feel about it (iykyk), and given the praise this game gets, I've had to ask myself whether or not I played the same one as everyone else.

The gameplay of E33 should technically also be a positive since I do like it, but I do have to critique it a bit. Combat has a central focus on parries. This in mind, you'd think parrying would be rewarding, but it really isn't. If you parry all 7 hits of a combo string, what do you get besides AP you can easily get anyway? You get a single counter. And if you miss a single one of your parries, you are denied this small luxury. And because Elden Ring and its consequences have been a complete disaster for the human race, the developers looked at that game and really admired how many obnoxiously delayed attacks were in it and copied some homework. Have fun waiting a full 5 seconds for that one attack to land only for it to come out instantly on the 6th second. So while I like the combat on paper, and most of the time in practice, it does walk a line between being satisfying and being annoying.

The dialogue in this game is usually good/fine, but weighed down by Marvel-esque quips and forced humor. You'll eventually hear characters use modern speech patterns and slang (I ♥♥♥♥ you not one of the characters says "Bromantic" + another moment where someone says "So which one is it?" only for another character to respond "Yes" in that funny internet way) to be "funny" and "lighten the mood." It's like the writers were told "make these characters feel real" and then they decided "characters feeling real" must equal "talks like a modern day person," which definitely doesn't break the tone or take you out of the setting or anything. The multiple palm prints on my face are the result of humorous dialogue, I assure you.

Humor has its place in a dark story and I don't dispute that fact. The problem with E33's "humor" is that it's so desperate to be funny that it constantly breaks the tone of the story and doesn't care that it does. It irked me to the point where I legitimately did begin to care less about the story/characters after one too many forced attempts at a laugh. Some of these moments land and feel like they have a place, but the vast majority don't. Hell, even a few of the expedition journals you can find about people who died are played off as jokes, and when you compare those journals to the intro of the game, you'll probably just narrow your eyes or cringe if anything.

Now for the story, as spoiler-free as possible:

You're introduced to the world with some good hooks, but sadly this game peaks at its intro and goes steadily downhill. Things are fine for a time until act 1's finale, during which some events take place seemingly just for cheap shock value (plus characters acting stupid for the sake of the plot) and fail to justify themselves any other way. Actually, it isn't even that shocking - odds are you'll be able to predict what happens long before it does, so it doesn't justify itself that way either. The events aren't "bad" in the moment, but looking back later in the game, you realize they happened for no reason other than to set the stage for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot twist. In the context of where the game goes, act 1's finale is garbage. It feels like someone said "Hey wouldn't it be cool/funny/random/shocking if we did this at this moment in the game?" and everyone just unanimously decided to throw it in for how quirky of an idea it was.

Act 2's finale is even worse and tries too hard to pull off an M Night Shyamalan twist to the point where it just feels super jarring and random. Think of the dumbest, most random plot twist a story can have and there's decent odds you just guessed THE major plot twist of E33, or close enough to it that I wouldn't be able to say you were wrong. Act 2's finale pulls the rug out from under you so it can say "Ha, gotcha!", then takes the story in a bizarre direction and proceeds to hide behind annoyingly contrived twists. And despite the fact that these events are the storytelling equivalent of upending a set table for fun, you're still expected to care about what happens next and participate in like 60 hours of sidequest hell to provide explanation as to what the ♥♥♥♥ you just witnessed and learn more about things you have no reason (and/or no longer have reason) to care about. Lmao no - I rushed the final boss because I was that out of ♥♥♥♥♥ to give. E33 was so focused on painting a plot twist that it didn't care whether or not what it painted made sense.

The start of act 2 and onwards feels like it was taken from a separate game idea and inserted clumsily into this one, with no regard given to whether or not it'd fit with the rest of the game, and all regard given to how unlikely it'd be for someone to guess the plot twist(s), which is obviously stupid writing that is doomed to sabotage any story and E33 is no exception. Given the previous points, my capacity to care about the rest of the story was already getting low, but I pressed onward hoping I'd see that life-changing masterpiece everyone talked about on the 25th hour or so only to run into act 2's finale and the game's ending(s) and encounter two middle fingers from the story as my reward. I wish my $40 a happy Gommage.

Act 2's finale punishes you for caring, and so do the endings, both of which are bad, but one of which is "moral"/"good" by the game's standards. That ending finishes what act 2's finale starts. To continue my "set table" analogy at risk of spoilers:[spoiler]It lights the upended table on fire because you were too attached to it and it wasn't a "real" table anyway. The other ending is resetting the table but putting mannequins in all the seats.[/spoiler] Both defeat the purpose of having a table. With how often you hear "for those who come after" in act 1, you'd think the story would continue that theme, but nope, it just shreds that in favor of a dumb plot twist that makes it ring hollow. The messages of the final act should flow well with the messages of the first but they're conveyed in the form of such convoluted twists that it feels more like the final act overwrites the first and doesn't pay off the story's hooks in a satisfying manner, destroying all intrigue, and rendering previous stakes and tension pointless.

And that is the most I can say spoiler-free. Everything else about the game is so well-presented, but the story and some of the dialogue are the exact opposite. I guess you could say that's a very "Clair Obscur" contrast.

I rarely put pen to digital paper for reviews, but some games demand it. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of those rare works—part storybook, part symphony, part duel of wills.

From the first step into its world, it’s clear the game has a painter’s hand behind it. The art, the music, the direction—everything feels crafted with the precision of someone who understands that style means nothing without substance. The story unfolds like a slow-burning folktale: tragic, strange, and full of humanity. Its pacing gives you room to breathe, to wander, to meet memorable faces—each one sketched with personality rather than clichés.

I came into this as a Souls veteran expecting familiar rhythms, and instead met a combat system that challenged my muscle memory. At first I doubted it. Then it swallowed me whole. The turn-based combat is nothing like the genre’s usual autopilot; it demands presence. Parries require timing as sharp as a razor, and a perfect parry feels like striking a bell in a cathedral—clean, resonant, earned. Dodges exist not as panic buttons but as teachers, helping you learn each enemy’s cadence.

Over time, the combat becomes meditative. In no-hit attempts, it borders on transcendence. You fall into a flow state where patience becomes your shield and emotional control your lifeline. This synchronicity between player and enemy is unlike anything I’ve felt in a turn-based system. It’s a combat language you learn, not a mechanic you exploit.

Exploration carries the same duality: grounded and playful. You can roam freely as any of your party members—up to three—and the game lets you switch perspectives at will. One moment you’re behind your character in third-person; the next you’re hovering overhead in a perspective reminiscent of classic RPGs or World of Warcraft. It’s a small touch, but it breathes life into wandering.

The RPG layer is surprisingly robust. Every character can be customized with outfits, hairstyles, weapon upgrades, and stat allocation. “Pictos” act as passive traits—tiny fragments of power that shift combat in clever ways—and choosing who gets what feels meaningful rather than obligatory. The game quietly encourages experimentation, offering multiple approaches to almost every encounter.

Performance? Impeccable. On my setup (i7-13620H, RTX 4060 Laptop GPU, 32GB DDR5, 1.5TB NVMe), the game didn’t flinch. No stutters, no hitches, no excuses. In a year full of broken releases, this one arrived polished and confident.

Here’s one nitpick: there’s no proper navigation or area map. Oddly enough, the absence of a good minimap or level overlay is that it forces you to pay attention to the streets, the architecture, the rhythm of each zone. Still, a few more environmental cues or subtle hints would’ve saved some backtracking. The compass is kind of useful and yes, there is a world map, but it's barely useful.

So here’s the truth: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 doesn’t just entertain. It moves. It offers a story worth hearing, music worth remembering, characters worth caring about, and a combat system worth mastering. It delivers challenge without cruelty, beauty without pretension, and heart without melodrama.

This isn’t simply a game; it’s an experience. A rare one. A memorable one.
If you care about games that try something bold—and actually succeed—then don’t skip this. Every penny is justified.
